activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: ProPublica, founded in 2007 as a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations, became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize, in 2010.
story:
Sebastian had spread the drafts of the Ledger's spring funding plan across the coffee table by seven, because at seven his mother stopped watching the local news and he could think. The living room smelled like burnt toast and lemon polish, and the TV was still murmuring the tail end of a segment about the paper mill closing, sponsored, said the voice, by Northgate Holdings. He noticed that the way it said Northgate Holdings was the same warm voice it used for the weather.

The problem in front of him was simple enough to verbalize in one sentence: the school paper had no money. Ads from the pizza place onRoute Nine had covered printing for years, but the pizza place was closing, and the faculty advisor, Ms. Moretti, had told the staff they either found new funding or printed nothing after April. At the last meeting Desirae had proposed selling ads to Northgate Holdings, since the company owned half the commercial property in town and could afford it. Ada had gone pale and said something about not biting the hand, and the two of them had argued until Ms. Moretti sent everyone home.

Sebastian's own position had started as a shrug. Money was money. But he kept circling back to the television, to that sponsor voice, to the fact that the mill closing was also a Northgate story, since Northgate had bought the mill two years ago and then shut it, and the local news had covered the closing the way it covered the weather, as a thing that happened to the town rather than a thing someone did. He wasn't ready to call it a machination. He was seventeen and he knew that word belonged to conspiracies, to men in rooms. Still, when he tried to imagine the paper running a hard story about Northgate with Northgate's logo on page two, something in the arrangement felt crooked before any person in it had done anything crooked.

He was still turning this over when Desirae came by with her laptop, having texted first that she had "ammunition." She sat on the end of the couch and pulled up a page. "Okay, counter-proposal. We don't sell ads at all. We ask for donations. Like this place." She turned the screen toward him. "ProPublica. It's a nonprofit newsroom, founded in 2007, funded by donations instead of ads. It won a Pulitzer in 2010, first online news source ever to do it." She said it fast, the way she recited stats before someone could interrupt. "So donors can work. It can be serious journalism, not a bake sale."

Ada arrived ten minutes later with her own counterargument, which was that donations weren't clean either. "Donors have opinions," she said, dropping onto the floor by the coffee table. "If the paper writes something a big donor hates, the big donor stops donating. It's the same leash, just softer." Desirae said that was cynical, and Ada said that being impervious to cynicism wasn't a virtue, and Sebastian, watching the two of them, realized he had been thinking about the whole thing wrong. He had been looking for a funding source with no interests at all, some neutral money, and maybe that was like looking for a sponsor with no voice.

He said as much, slowly, testing it while he spoke. "There's no clean option. Ads come with owners. Donations come with donors. Even no money comes with its own problems, because then we print nothing." Desirae argued that the ProPublica example showed the difference was real, not imaginary: a nonprofit could win a Pulitzer, could do the hardest kind of journalism there was. Ada allowed that, but she pointed out that ProPublica was national and famous, and their donors gave to the reputation, whereas the Ledger would have maybe eleven donors, most of them parents, and every one of them would know exactly which kid wrote which story.

Ms. Moretti had told them to come to Monday's meeting with a recommendation, so a recommendation had to exist, and Sebastian wrote one out in pencil on the back of the funding plan while Desirae and Ada kept going across the room. Take small donations from many people, cap any single donor at twenty dollars, put every donor's name in the back pages of every issue, and if Northgate ever offered an ad, the whole staff would vote on it in the open. Ada said that was a lot of ceremony for a paper with a circulation of four hundred. Desirae said she liked it, which surprised him, since it was half a retreat from her own plan.

Later, after the others had gone, he watched the eleven o'clock news come back on, the same anchor, the same warm voice reading Northgate's name. He knew what he had and what he didn't. He had a proposal, not a proof. Donors could still shape things, quietly, in ways no list of names would ever show, and he couldn't claim the Ledger's plan would work when nothing like it had been tried at their scale. What he had, really, was a way of noticing: that money always speaks, and the best you could do was make it speak out loud.

He gathered the pages, stacked them, and reached for the remote. Then he stopped, because the anchor was reading the next sponsor's name, and it was the pizza place on Route Nine, the one that was supposedly closing, thanking the community for nineteen years of support.

"We're not going anywhere," the owner said in the sound bite that followed, grinning behind the counter. "Spring renovation, that's all it is."

Sebastian sat back down on the couch, the remote forgotten in his hand, and watched the rest of the segment without blinking.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: A 2005 study by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness.
story:
The waiting room smelled of toner and cold coffee, and the chair beneath Liam had a plastic squeak that announced every shift of his weight. He sat with his hands flat on his knees, wearing a shirt his mother had ironed while telling him, for the fourth time, that the research assistant job at the county health office would look good on a college application. Through the frosted glass door he could hear a voice, level and unhurried, the voice of a man asking someone else questions. Liam mouthed his own answers under his breath. He had written them out the night before, bullet points in a notebook, because Kira had told him that structured answers landed better than rambling ones, and because he had learned, recently and painfully, that he could not trust his instincts about how his words would sound to a stranger.

The door opened and a girl came out, flushed and quick. Mr. Paquette appeared behind her in a grey cardigan, older than Liam had expected, with reading glasses pushed up into white hair. "Liam?" he said, checking a clipboard. "Come in. Take the window chair if you want the light."

The office was small and papered with charts. One of them, Liam noticed as he sat, was a map of the county with colored dots clustered in the eastern towns. "That's our influenza surveillance," Mr. Paquette said, following his eyes. "You'd be helping compile the weekly reports, if you're the one we pick. Mostly data entry, some drafting. The epidemiology team sends numbers; you turn them into summaries the public can read."

"Summaries," Liam repeated. "Like, paragraphs?"

"Like paragraphs with a shape. A finding, the evidence, what it means, what it doesn't mean." Mr. Paquette settled behind the desk. "Most of your work will be email, honestly. Telling clinics what we need, answering their questions. Tone matters in that work. You'd be the voice of the office." He said it lightly, but he watched Liam as he said it.

Liam thought of Kira in the school library in October, both of them hunched over her laptop, the overhead lights buzzing, the smell of old bindings and lemon disinfectant. She had been reading about a 2005 study by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and some colleagues, and she had pushed the screen toward him. The writers of emails, she said, wildly overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, whether they're being sarcastic or serious. Senders think they've made themselves clear and they haven't. Liam had laughed at the time and said something like, who doesn't know when I'm joking? She had looked at him a beat too long before answering, and he had pretended not to notice the look.

"Tell me about a time you handled a disagreement," Mr. Paquette said now.

Liam had prepared for this one, and he gave it the shape he'd rehearsed: the situation, what he did, the result. In his senior English seminar he had disagreed with a classmate's reading of a poem, and instead of arguing in circles he had written out his position in three sentences, cited two lines of the poem, and let the teacher moderate. "It went better than talking over each other," Liam said. "Writing it down forced me to be fair to her side. I couldn't just wave my hands." Mr. Paquette nodded slowly, making a note, and Liam felt something in his chest unclench a fraction.

"One more thing," Mr. Paquette said, and turned the clipboard toward him. "Your writing sample was strong. The cover letter, less so. There was an exchange with a manager, forwarded to us by your reference at the pool. You wrote, and I quote, 'Great, another Saturday shift, exactly what I always wanted.'" He took off his glasses. "That was intended as a joke, I assume."

The room went very still. The radiator ticked. Somewhere down the hall a printer ground through a cycle, and Liam could hear his own pulse in his ears, the whole walk home from the pool that evening replaying itself: the manager's flat reply, the shift he had still worked, the silence he had told himself meant nothing. He had meant it as a joke. He had assumed the manager would hear it as one. That was the exact mistake, he understood now, the one Kira had shown him under the buzzing library lights, and he had walked right into it anyway, two weeks later, as if reading about a hole in the ice entitled him to fall through it.

"Yes," Liam said. "It was a joke. Badly judged. I found out afterward that he read it as me complaining, and I understand why. There was research I could have paid attention to before I hit send." He kept his voice level, the way the interview itself had taught him, in these last ten minutes, that a voice could be. "I should have apologized in plain words, no irony, and I did go back and do that. It took me too long."

Mr. Paquette studied him for a moment. Liam, who had rehearsed a smooth answer about teamwork, found he no longer wanted to prevaricate, to dress the thing up in softer language. "You know," Mr. Paquette said, "half the applicants would have blamed the manager's sense of humor." He made another note. "The job is mostly ancillary to the actual science, mind you. You'd be support, not discovery. Reports, emails, filing. Some people find that boring."

"I find that's where the mistakes happen," Liam said. "The small communications. That's what I got wrong, so that's what I'd actually be careful about." He heard his own certainty and tested it, the way he'd learned to test a claim in the seminar, and found it held. He had walked in wanting to seem polished; he was leaving the interview wanting something else, and the change had happened somewhere between the map of colored dots and the forwarded email.

Mr. Paquette walked him to the door. Outside, the parking lot had gone bright with late afternoon, heat shimmering off the hoods of cars, and Liam squinted into it. He was halfway to his bike when he turned back. The window of the office was open an inch, and Mr. Paquette was standing at it with the clipboard.

"If you get it," Mr. Paquette called down, "your first email draft goes to me before you send it."

"Deal," Liam said. "I'll write it boring on purpose."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: Bigger samples help less than people expect: doubling a random sample from 1,000 to 2,000 people shrinks the margin of error by only about one percentage point.
story:
Brayden had volunteered at the campaign office because he believed in civic engagement, which was partly true and partly the fact that Ismael had a car and Ismael was going. Either way, by the second Saturday he considered himself essential, and by the third he had said so out loud, twice.

The office was a rented storefront between a nail salon and a place that sold phone cases, and it smelled like toner and the fundraiser subs someone kept ordering. On the back wall, taped at a careless angle, hung a printout of the latest poll. The candidate trailed by four points, and beneath the number, in small gray type, sat the phrase margin of error, plus or minus three. Brayden had walked past it all morning without reading it, which was unusual, because he considered himself a person who read things.

Mohamed-Amine wanted to double the phone calls. That was the whole drama of the afternoon. He stood at the folding table with a marker and a piece of poster board on which he had written CALL GOAL: 1,000 and then, after some deliberation, crossed it out and written 2,000. "If we call twice as many people," he said, "the poll gets accurate. It's math. The subs guy told me the poll only talked to a thousand people, which is basically nothing."

"It's not nothing," Brayden said, mostly because Mohamed-Amine's confidence annoyed him, and only partly because he knew anything.

"It's one high school. You're telling me one high school picks the mayor?"

Ismael, who was texting someone, said, without looking up, "It's random. That's the whole point. It's like soup." He went back to his phone, having delivered this, and did not elaborate, and both of them hated him a little.

Brayden took the marker and drew a line through the 2,000 and wrote 1,000 back, and Mohamed-Amine looked at him like he had vandalized a church. So Brayden went to prove it, which required finding out whether it was true, which he did not mention. On the shelf under the coffee maker was a binder the field organizer had left, and in the binder was a chart of sample sizes and their margins of error, printed from somewhere, no author, no lecture attached. He ran his finger down the column. One thousand people, plus or minus three. Two thousand people, plus or minus two.

He read it twice. He had assumed doubling would cut the error in half, and it didn't, and he sat with that for a moment on an overturned milk crate.

"Look," he said, bringing the binder over, because there was no way to admit he'd been guessing without also admitting he'd been guessing. "Double it from a thousand to two thousand and the margin only drops by about one point. Three becomes two. That's it. Two thousand calls buys you one point."

Mohamed-Amine frowned at the chart. "So what do we do?"

"I don't know yet. Make the calls anyway, I guess. Just don't pretend it's magic." This came out more generous than Brayden felt, since he had wanted, ten minutes earlier, roughly the same magic. The disaffected voters they'd been reaching all week, the ones who said nothing changes so why answer the phone, weren't going to be un-disaffected by arithmetic. He thought about saying that and didn't, because it sounded like a poster.

Mr. Villanueva, the retired teacher who organized Saturdays and referred to everyone as "champ," came by with the sub box. He glanced at the poster board, at the crossed-out numbers stacked on each other like failed traffic signs. "Doubling the calls, huh. You'd have to do a lot more than double before that margin really moves." He took a sub and left, having said almost nothing, which Brayden found suspicious in a man that cheerful.

They made the calls. Brayden got a man who wanted to commodify his attention, four dollars a minute, and a woman who spoke in a vernacular of sighs, and a kid who said his parents weren't home and could Brayden call back never. The tally sheet crept toward three hundred. Mohamed-Amine, dialing beside him, said, "One point. For a thousand calls." He said it the way you'd say the price of something.

"Some of the calls aren't for the poll," Brayden said. "Some of them are for the campaign. Those count differently." He was not sure this was true. He had decided, provisionally, that the honest position was somewhere between the soup theory and the subs guy, and that he would hold it until Friday, when the next poll came out, and the candidate was still down four, still plus or minus three, and the nail salon's neon sign blinked on through the window in the dark.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Haggadah is the book read aloud at a Passover Seder; it retells the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt.
story:
The box arrived on Thursday, and the Seder was Saturday night, which left Logan two days to learn what his grandfather used to carry in his head. His mother had said it plainly at dinner, without ceremony: this year you lead, since Pop was gone and she couldn't do it alone. Inside the box were thirty mismatched Haggadot, ordered used from three different sellers, some with wine rings on their covers, one with a grandmother's handwriting in the margins. Logan spread them across the kitchen table like evidence.

"It's the book we read aloud from," his mother said, passing him with a stack of plates. "Start to finish. It retells the whole story, the Israelites leaving slavery in Egypt." Then she was gone into the pantry, and he was alone with the copies, opening the first one and realizing how long it actually was. Forty, fifty pages of Hebrew and English wound together, songs in the back, instructions in italics he didn't understand. Two days.

He texted Rafaelle, whose family did this every year and who had, in Logan's memory, always looked bored at the table. Rafaelle showed up Friday after school with Amine, who wasn't Jewish at all but came for the food and stayed for the argument. "You don't read all of it," Rafaelle said, flipping pages with the ease of someone who had memorized the shape of it if not the words. "You go around the table. Everybody gets a turn." Amine leaned over the book. "So it's like a relay," he said. "Nobody runs the whole race alone."

That was the part that mesmerized Logan, once he saw it. The Haggadah wasn't a speech one person delivered; it was a script distributed across a table, and the leader's job wasn't to perform but to portion. He spent Friday evening with a yellow marker, deciding which passages to hand out and to whom. His mother's uncle, who read slowly and grandly, would get the ten plagues, which were dramatic enough to survive a slow delivery. His little cousin Dara, who was nine and wanted, had announced at least six times, "a real part, not the baby part," would get the four questions. He wrote her name next to them and then second-guessed it, because the four questions were the centerpiece, and if she froze the whole table would sit in the silence.

Saturday morning he walked to Mr. Ortiz's apartment above the bakery, because Mr. Ortiz had run large events for years and knew something about crowds, any crowds. "You're serving twenty people," Mr. Ortiz said, counting on his fingers, "which means twenty people who can each ruin it or save it. Which one is your worry?" Logan said it was Dara. Mr. Ortiz nodded slowly. "Then you rehearse her. Not the part. Her. Come by at four."

At four, Dara sat on Mr. Ortiz's sofa with the marked-up Haggadah and read the four questions out loud, twice, while Mr. Ortiz pretended to be a difficult guest, checking his watch, asking for more juice. Dara giggged, lost her place, found it, read again. Logan watched her shoulders drop an inch each time through. He also noticed something he hadn't expected: she had opinions. She wanted the passage about the wise son because she thought she was the wise son, and she asked Logan whether he got to choose who was wise and who was wicked, or whether the book decided. He said he honestly didn't know. The book seemed to sort people into types, and the table would have to sort itself.

Amine arrived at five with matzah he had bought himself, "for practice," and sat with Logan while the soup simmered, and it was Amine who raised the thing Logan had been circling all day. "So the whole point is remembering being slaves," Amine said, turning the book toward the window light. "But you guys are comfortable. Is that a problem, or is that the point?" Logan thought about it while peeling an egg for the seder plate. He said maybe the story worked like an externality his economics teacher kept describing, a cost someone else paid long ago that still landed on your table, and you couldn't give it back, only notice it. Amine considered this, then said the noticing had better be worth something, otherwise it was just guilt with soup.

At seven, people filled the chairs, and Logan stood, and his stomach did the thing it does. He poured the first cup, said the blessing the way the phonetic guide in the margin had drilled into him, and started passing out the marked pages. His great-uncle got the plagues and did exactly what Logan had predicted, drawing out each one like weather. When they reached the four questions, Dara stood up without being asked. She read them too fast, then too slow, then found the rhythm, and the table went quiet in the way Logan had been afraid of, except it wasn't ruin, it was the opposite of ruin, and he understood only then that those might be the same silence.

The night was not perfect. An aunt argued that skipping a section was "watering down the whole thing," and Rafaelle, across the table, defended the cuts, and Logan let them argue for a minute before moving on, because he had decided that leading sometimes meant letting the table talk. When they reached the part where the door is opened for the prophet Elijah, Dara opened it onto the cold hallway and stood in the doorway, staring out as if she actually expected someone, and Logan found he was staring too.

"Next year," his mother said quietly, refilling his cup, "you'll cut it differently." Logan looked down the table at the wine rings forming on the cloth, at Amine already buttering matzah he wasn't supposed to butter yet, and folded his page corner. "Next year I'll ask Dara first."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought The Washington Post from the Graham family in 2013 for $250 million.
story:
The radiator in the student newspaper office clanked at intervals nobody had ever successfully predicted, and Liam had learned to save his work between clanks. He was pasting the last of his article into the layout, a piece about the cafeteria contract switching to a new supplier, when Ryley spun a laptop toward him across the cluttered desk. "Look at this. The Post did this whole investigation into working conditions, and it's actually good, but check who owns it."

Liam read the line Ryley was pointing at, a small disclosure at the bottom of a Washington Post story about Amazon warehouses. He read it twice. The Post's owner was Amazon's founder, Jeff Bezos, who had bought the paper from the Graham family in 2013 for $250 million. Two hundred and fifty million. Liam thought about what a school, a city block, a life cost, and then about what a newspaper with a century of history cost, and the numbers refused to sit next to each other in any comfortable way.

"So does that mean the story's fake?" Ryley asked. "Or that it's extra real, because they ran it anyway?"

"That's not the question." Heidi came in with her bag still on her shoulder, shaking rain off her jacket. She was the editor and had opinions the way the radiator had steam. "The question is what they choose to cover, not just how they cover it. A paper can be honest about everything it prints and still decide some things aren't worth printing."

Liam looked at his own article on the screen. The cafeteria supplier. He had been proud of it an hour ago, mostly because it was factual, careful, and insouciant in a way he thought read as confidence. Now the pride felt thinner. Their paper was owned by nobody, technically, funded by the school through Mr. Guo's budget sign-offs, and Mr. Guo answered to a principal who cared deeply about the school's image. He had never once thought of that as ownership. It had just seemed like the way things were.

Heidi dropped her bag on the chair beside him and pulled the laptop closer, reading the disclosure herself. From where she stood, she could see the problem land on Liam in slow motion, the way it had landed on her a year ago during a fight over a story about the swim team. She had wanted to run it; the coach had called it divisive, and someone upstairs had used the word "unbalanced," and the story had died in a drawer. She had learned then to dichotomize less, to stop splitting the world into captured media and free media, because the truth was a sliding scale and everyone sat somewhere on it. What she hadn't figured out was how to tell Liam that without making him want to quit before he'd started.

"You're wondering if your supplier story is dead on arrival," she said.

"Is it?"

"No. It's wondering whether you are." She tapped the screen. "Bezos bought it, yeah. And they still publish things that make his company look bad sometimes, and they also soft-pedal things sometimes, probably, and neither of those proves anything on its own. You don't get certainty here, Liam. You get judgment."

Mr. Guo appeared in the doorway with the budget folder under his arm, which was his way of saying the office had to be locked by six. He glanced at the article header over Liam's shoulder and said nothing, which was itself a kind of data. Liam saved the file, then opened a new document and typed a single line at the top: who decides what we cover, and why. It wasn't a story yet. It might be a column, or a question at the next budget meeting, or nothing. Below it he typed a second line, the fact Ryley had found, the year, the price, the family that sold, copied exactly so he couldn't get it wrong later.

Ryley leaned over. "You're actually going to write about this?"

"I'm going to try," Liam said, and hit print.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election.
story:
The line outside the community hall moved in short stops, and Lucas stood behind a woman in a quilted coat who kept checking her watch. He had his registration card folded into his back pocket, though he had read that he did not need it, and he touched it anyway every few minutes, the way he used to check for his bus pass on the first week of school, before he had acclimated to the route.

Oskar was already inside, leaning against the folding table where a woman with a lanyard was handing out ballots. Oskar had turned eighteen in March and had announced for weeks that he was not going to bother. "Half of us don't even show up," he said now, following Lucas toward the booths. "If half the people our age can't be bothered, what's my one vote worth?"

"That's the wrong way to count it," Lucas said. He had looked it up two nights ago, after Ronald had said the same thing in the group chat. "CIRCLE. It's a research center at Tufts. They estimated that fifty percent of Americans aged eighteen to twenty-nine voted in the 2020 presidential election." He said it flatly, the way he had read it, because he had learned that if he dressed the number up, Oskar heard only the dressing.

"Fifty percent," Oskar repeated. "So half of us did show up."

"Half did. Half didn't. Same fact." Lucas took a ballot from the woman with the lanced fingers of someone who had been dealing paper all day. "You're using the half that stayed home as your excuse. I'm standing in the half that came."

Oskar made a sound that was not agreement and not refusal. He took a ballot too.

The booths were cardboard dividers on metal legs, and the pen was tied to the frame with a length of yarn. Lucas read every line before marking anything. He had argued about two of these races with Ronald, who wanted to vote a straight ticket and be done in ninety seconds, and with his mother, who read the county judge candidates like she was auditing them. He had started out repeating his mother's reasoning, then found himself defending Ronald's, and had finally gone through the sample ballot alone on Thursday night with no one's voice in his head, which turned out to be harder than either. There was one race, for the water district board, where he still did not know. He left that one blank and did not feel good about it, and marked the rest.

When he came out, Ms. Ba was sitting at a table near the door with a clipboard and a badge that said she was an observer. She taught government at the high school and had retired the year before. He knew her from the model congress club, which she had run for a small honorarium, fifteen dollars a session, which she had once mentioned with a laugh while locking up the classroom.

"First time," she said. It was not a question; she had watched him read the ballot for eleven minutes. "Did you vote the whole sheet?"

"Most of it." He did not say which part he had skipped, and she did not ask.

Outside the light had gone crepuscular, the parking lot lamps coming on against a sky still holding some blue. Ronald was leaning on the hood of his car, phone in hand, and he called out before Lucas reached him. "Did it in under two minutes. Straight ticket. You?"

"I read it all," Lucas said. "Skipped one."

Ronald shook his head, but he was grinning, and Oskar came out the door behind them holding his stub like a receipt he intended to keep. "Fifty percent," Oskar said, to no one in particular. "I keep thinking about how that's half of everyone I know."

"Both halves," Lucas said.

Ronald unlocked the car and they got in, the three of them, and Ronald pulled out of the lot while Oskar was still reading his stub under the dome light.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
Antoine arrived at the field before anyone else, as he had every morning that August, and set out the cones in the same lines his coach used, orange against the alluvial green of the grass where the drainage ditch had flooded in June. He ran the drill again. He had stopped bothering to time himself, because the times had been getting worse for two weeks and he did not want to see the numbers.

Junior found him at the halfway line, breathing hard, hands on his knees. "You're here every day," Junior said, not as praise. "Karis told me you were. She said you didn't take Sunday off either."

"Season starts in three weeks," Antoine said. "I can't afford a day off."

Junior sat down on the ball, which Antoine found rude in a way he couldn't name. "My cousin ran cross-country. She trained every day and got slower, and then a physio made her take days off and she got faster. I never understood it until Karis showed me the word." He pulled his phone from his sock, opened a page, and held it out. "It's called supercompensation."

Antoine read the screen twice. The body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself. He looked up at Junior, then at the cones he had laid out, then at his own legs, which ached in a low, constant way he had stopped noticing. "That can't be right," he said. "You get better by working."

"That's what my cousin thought too."

Karis arrived with a notebook, because Karis arrived everywhere with a notebook, and when Antoine told her what Junior had said she sat down on the grass and opened it. "So draw the week," she said. "If the rebuilding happens after, then the day you skip is doing the work. Monday hard, Tuesday easy, Wednesday hard, Thursday off. Write it down and stop arguing with it."

Antoine took the pencil but didn't write. It felt like a trick, like an aphorism someone had made up to make laziness sound scientific, the kind of thing printed on a poster in the gym. "My dad says rest is for people who don't want it enough."

"Your dad also says headers don't cause concussions," Karis said, not unkindly, and Junior laughed, and Antoine laughed too, and then, because it was easier than admitting he was afraid of losing ground, he wrote MONDAY: SPRINTS. TUESDAY: EASY. WEDNESDAY: SPRINTS. THURSDAY: NOTHING. He wrote WARM-UP and STRETCH at the top of every day as well, because Karis pointed out that a cold muscle was a stupid reason to lose a week, and even his father couldn't argue with that.

The hardest part was Thursday. He walked to the field anyway, out of habit, and stood at the gate watching the empty grass where his cones should have been, and it physically hurt, some animal part of him certain that everyone else was out there getting better while he stood still. A neighbour, Mr. Popescu, was walking his dog along the touchline and stopped beside him. "Injury?" Mr. Popescu asked, nodding at Antoine's trackspare legs.

"Rest day," Antoine said. "Planned."

"Ah." Mr. Popescu whistled the dog back toward the path. "I took up gardening at fifty and learned the same thing about soil. You can't keep taking out." He left before Antoine could decide whether that was wisdom or an accident of phrasing.

The following Monday, Karis timed him. The first sprint was ordinary. The second was better. The third was the fastest he had run since the tests in spring, and Junior, standing at the far cone, extruded the stopwatch arm from beneath his hoodie like it was the only thing on the field that mattered, and shouted the time loud enough that two boys playing five-a-side at the other end turned to look. Antoine walked a slow circle, pretending his lungs were the reason he couldn't speak.

"So the plan works," Karis said, pen hovering over the notebook.

Antoine looked down the field at the two boys, one of whom was clearly exhausted and clearly not stopping, sprinting again and again while his friend called for him to ease off. He recognized the posture, the set of the shoulders, the refusal to look at the bench. "It works," he said. "Wait here."

He jogged over, boots clicking on the hard dirt at the edge of the pitch, and stood where the boy would have to notice him. "Hey," Antoine said. "You want to see something? It's about your days off."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution in his 1863 book on drama technique.
story:
Sophia's mother dropped her at the community theatre at nine in the morning with a notebook and a thermos of coffee, and by ten Sophia had written four hundred words about the day her grandfather died, none of which she believed. Ms. Pérez had set the assignment on Monday: a ten-minute play drawn from the writer's own life, staged on the last Friday of the workshop with the other students as actors. "Not a memoir," Ms. Pérez had said. "A play. Something has to happen." Sophia had underlined the phrase twice and then avoided thinking about it for four days.

The theatre was an old converted fire hall with folding chairs and a smell of dust and glue. Lynden had claimed the corner table near the coffee urn and was sketching on a napkin with a ballpoint pen. When Sophia came over, he turned the napkin toward her. He had drawn a triangle, divided into five horizontal bands, and labelled them from the bottom up: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.

"Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid like this," Lynden said, tapping the triangle with the pen. "Exposition at the base, climax at the peak, resolution back down at the base. He wrote it up in 1863, in his book on drama technique." He had looked it up the night before, he admitted, because his own draft kept stalling in the middle and he wanted to know where things were supposed to go.

Sophia copied the napkin into her notebook. Her grandfather piece, she could see immediately, was all exposition: the hospital room, the crepuscular light through the blinds, the relatives arriving in order of distance driven. Nothing rose. She sat with that for a while, watching Mckayla pace the stage and read her own script aloud in different voices.

At lunch Mckayla sat down across from her with a bagel and asked what Sophia was writing about. "The night my grandfather died," Sophia said, and then, because Mckayla kept waiting, "I wasn't there. I was at a debate tournament. I found out in the car on the way home." Mckayla said that was the play. Sophia said no, the play was about him. Mckayla took a bite of bagel and said that nobody on stage could play a dead man for ten minutes.

The argument carried into the afternoon. Sophia held that writing about her own absence was self-flattery, a way of putting herself at the centre of a story that belonged to someone else. Lynden, still hovering over his napkin pyramid, pointed out that the climax of a play is not the most important event in the world of the play but the moment of greatest pressure on the person we're watching. "The climax is the peak," he said. "The peak of Freytag's pyramid. It's where the rising action stops rising." Sophia thought about probity, a word she'd learned for the SATs and never used, and how her insistence on writing only the hospital room was less like honesty than like its costume. The honest thing might be the car, the phone lighting up, the coach's voice on the radio saying something stupid about traffic.

She started a new draft in the third hour. Two characters in a car: a girl and a driver she called the aunt. The girl has her phone turned face-down on her knee and knows, in the way you know before you're told, what the missed calls mean. The rising action was the girl asking the aunt to check the phone and the aunt saying after we park, after we park. Sophia wrote the climax as the girl picking up the phone at a red light and reading four messages in order, the fourth one only two words long. She didn't write what the words were.

Lynden read it over her shoulder and said the falling action was thin. Sophia said she didn't know what happened after, in real life, except that they sat in the parked car for a long time and that her mother had a way of handling grief that other people found cold and that she had spent a year defending to herself. She didn't want to write a scene that stigmatized the mother for not crying, but she also didn't want to fake tears she hadn't seen. "Then leave it unresolved," Ms. Pérez said, passing behind them with a armful of extension cords. "Resolution doesn't mean answered. Freytag built the pyramid for five-act tragedies. You have ten minutes."

On Friday Sophia's play was performed in the folding-chair rows under work lights. Mckayla played the girl with the phone held low, out of the aunt's sightline, and the audience, which was mostly parents, went quiet at the red light. The final image Sophia had written was the two of them in the parked car, the engine off, the aunt's hands still at ten and two on a steering wheel that wasn't going anywhere. It held for eight seconds and then the work lights came up.

Afterward her mother found her by the coffee urn. She said the car scene was accurate, which from her was a long speech. Then she said, "I never sat like that afterward, with my hands on the wheel." Sophia said she knew, that she'd made that part up, that she wasn't sure yet whether it was a lie or just the shape the truth needed. Her mother considered the coffee urn for a moment and then filled her cup from the dregs at the bottom.

"Show me the napkin thing," her mother said. "The pyramid. Lynden's mother told me about it." Sophia dug out her notebook, found the page with the copied triangle, and flattened it on the urn's warm metal lid, tracing the five bands once with her finger, base to peak to base.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Ontario combines the federal GST with its provincial sales tax into a single 13 percent Harmonized Sales Tax, shown as one HST line on receipts.
story:
Isaac had been sent to Ms. Kaya's office because his mother worked Saturdays now and someone had to carry the folder of papers, the receipts in a rubber-banded envelope, the T4 slip with its pale green edges. Ms. Kaya had an office above a dry cleaner on Danforth Avenue, one room with two chairs, a filing cabinet, and a window that looked out on the awning of a Portuguese bakery. She waved him into the second chair while she went through the envelope, and Isaac, who had nothing to do but watch, watched.

The receipts came out first. Ms. Kaya laid them on the desk in a line, and Isaac noticed that each one had a single tax line at the bottom, one amount, thirteen percent of the subtotal, no more. He thought of his uncle's stories about Montreal, where he said you needed a second line, a separate provincial tax stacked on top of the federal one. Here there was only ever one. "One line," he said, almost to himself, touching the receipt from the restaurant where his mother had taken him in March for his birthday.

"Harmonized Sales Tax," Ms. Kaya said, without looking up, the way she might have named a plant on a windowsill. She tapped the bottom of the receipt, where it said HST, and moved on to the next paper.

Isaac sat with that. Thirteen percent, and the federal and provincial parts arrived together, fused into one figure, the way his mother's paycheque fused several things into one deduction. He asked if he could see the paycheque stub, and she slid it across the desk. At the top, his mother's gross pay for the two-week period; beneath it, lines for income tax, both federal and provincial, plus amounts for Canada Pension Plan and employment insurance; and at the bottom, the net, the number that actually reached the bank. He had never realized the two taxes were listed separately there, split apart, while on the receipt they were joined. He wondered which arrangement was more honest, one number that was easier to read or two that were easier to check.

The door opened and Frederic came in with his own folder, sent by his father, who believed in errands as character formation. Frederic dropped into the corner and started narrating his misfortunes, which were epicurean in scale, as he put it: he had spent his entire pay from the grocery store on takeout and had nothing left for the concert in June. He wanted to know whether there was a way to get it back, some refund for suffering. "Not for takeout," Ms. Kaya said. She explained, briefly, that his employer had already withheld income tax from his cheques, more than he likely owed at his earnings, and that when he filed his return the excess would come back to him. Frederic brightened visibly. "So they take it and then give it back?" "If they took too much," she said.

Isaac found himself arguing, gently, that this was not the outrage Frederic was making it. The withholding was a kind of saving you didn't have to decide on, money sublimated out of sight before it could become takeout. Frederic said that was exactly the problem; he would rather have his own thirteen percent, or his own twenty, and choose. Isaac pointed at the receipt line again, the single tax, and said that whether the money left in one stream or two, the same amount left. Frederic said that wasn't the point, and Isaac conceded it maybe wasn't.

Ms. Kaya, meanwhile, was working through the return itself, entering figures from the T4, subtracting deductions, the union dues and a small amount for safety boots, from the income before applying the tax rates. Isaac watched the numbers on her screen rearrange themselves and understood, for the first time in a concrete way, that taxable income was a smaller thing than income, that the form carved away certain costs before it asked its question. He did not fully understand which costs counted and which did not, and he was honest with himself about that; the rules had a logic he could see the edge of but not the whole shape of.

When Ms. Kaya finished, she told him his mother was owed a refund, modest but real, and printed a page to be signed. Frederic, still in the corner, had found the bakery downstairs on his phone and was reading out the prices of pastries, adding the tax in his head out loud, one figure, thirteen percent, correct every time.

Outside, on the sidewalk under the awning, Isaac folded the signed page into the envelope. Frederic was already holding the door of the bakery open. "You're buying," Frederic said, "you're the one with the refund."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A table read is a seated read-through of a script by the cast, used to hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins.
story:
The auditorium smelled like dust and radiator paint, and Ms. Hosseini had pushed six folding chairs into a rough circle on the stage because the seats out front were too far away for what she called listening. Connor sat with his script on his knee, twelve pages, the longest thing he had ever finished. He had written it about the night his father missed his regional semifinal, though the play said it was about a boy and a man and a bus that never came, which he felt was different in an important way he could not have named.

"It's a table read," Ms. Hosseini said, sitting down. "Seated, scripts in hand. We hear how the dialogue sounds before anyone stands up and stages anything."

Mandy had the boy's part. Zaynab had the man's. Connor had asked for no part at all, and then had been given the bus announcer, which was one line.

They began. For the first two pages the play was fine, which is to say nothing happened to him while it went by. He heard Mandy say the boy's opening lines and thought, that's not quite my voice, and then thought, well, it isn't my voice, it's the boy's, and settled into the distinction the way you settle into a chair that almost fits.

Then Zaynab read the line where the man explains why he missed the game. "I valorize your persistence more than any trophy," Zaynab read, flatly, obediently, and the whole circle went quiet in the specific way that a room goes quiet when nobody wants to be the one to say it.

Connor had written that line at one in the morning and felt extremely literary writing it. Hearing it, he understood that no father stuck at a bus stop at nine at night had ever said the word valorize to anyone, and that the line was a costume he had put on the moment so it would look more serious than it was. His face did something he tried to control. Ms. Hosseini saw it anyway, because she was circumspect about most things but not about watching students' faces during their own plays.

"Notes," she said, when they finished. "But the writer goes first, and the writer has to say one true thing."

"It's not how he talks," Connor said. "Any of it, that whole speech. I made him sound like a letter to the editor." He was quiet for a second. "I think I did it because the real version was smaller. He just said sorry and asked if I won, and I was mad that sorry was all there was, so I gave him a philosophy."

Zaynab, who was eating crackers she had smuggled in her script folder, said, "So write the sorry."

"But the sorry is worse. The sorry just sits there." He turned a page, not reading it. "In bio we just did speciation, how a population splits until they can't interbreed anymore, and I keep thinking that's what happened. Him and me. Same house, and then a canyon opens up somewhere in the middle of it, and nobody announces it, you just find out one night that you're different species now. And I want the play to say both things. That he failed me, and that the canyon is real, and that I can't prove the canyon wasn't partly my digging." He stopped, aware he had said more than the room needed. "Sorry. The crackers smell good."

Mandy said, "Read the sorry line. I'll do the kid part."

Zaynab put down her crackers. "I'm sorry, kiddo. Did you win?"

"We lost by two," Mandy read. "It went to overtime."

"Overtime," Zaynab said, as if tasting the word.

Nobody said anything after that, but it was a different silence from before, and Ms. Hosseini did not fill it, only looked at the margin of her script where she had written something Connor couldn't see upside down. He looked at his twelve pages and did not know yet which of them would survive, only that the costume was coming off and he didn't know what the man underneath would sound like, or whether he would still recognize him. He clicked his pen and crossed out the whole speech.

"Okay," he said. "From the top of page three. And Zaynab, keep the crackers away from my script, it's the only copy."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
Clara counted the bills in her wallet twice before she reached the front of the line, because the roast was eleven dollars more than she had planned for and the rest of the market still had things she needed. The vendor, a woman with flour on her forearms, waited without hurrying her. Behind Clara, Ziyad shifted his canvas bag from one shoulder to the other and said, "I can lend it."

"No," Clara said. "It's my dinner to cook. I'm not being bailed out by my sous chef."

"Delegate," Ziyad said. "It's a leadership skill."

She paid, took the wrapped roast, and put it in the cooler she had brought with a frozen bottle in it, because they still had to find thyme and bread and the honey her mother had asked for, and meat left in a car in August was a project that would incapacitate the whole evening. Ziyad wrote the list on his phone. He was better at lists than she was; she was better at plans, and the plan was this: her parents' anniversary, her mother working until six, her father pretending he had not reminded her three times, and Clara cooking the meal her parents had eaten on their first anniversary, which her mother had described once, in passing, and which Clara had reconstructed from that passing description like an archaeologist with one shard.

"Rosemary or thyme?" Ziyad asked at the herb table.

"Thyme. She said thyme."

"She said thyme once, in passing, in March."

"I remember passing things," Clara said. "It's the permanent things I lose."

They found Jaida at the honey stall, arguing mildly with the beekeeper about whether buckwheat honey was too truculent for a glaze, and when Clara asked her to settle it, Jaida said, "Buckwheat is an acquired temperament. Some people never acquire it." Clara bought the wildflower anyway, because her mother had said wildflower, or because wildflower was safer, or because at some point a decision had to be made and this was the shape it took.

At home the kitchen was hot by four. Clara trimmed the roast, seared it in the pan her mother used for everything, rubbed it with the thyme and garlic and a paste of honey and mustard that was not in her mother's description but that Clara thought of as her own small amendment, an amalgam of the remembered meal and her own instincts, which was either a betrayal of the idea or the only way an idea stays alive. Ziyad set the table. Jaida, who had come over with the honey and stayed, peeled potatoes and asked whether this was a surprise or a performance.

"Both," Clara said. "A surprise for them. A performance for me."

She had looked up the temperature the night before, written it on the back of a receipt that now hung by a magnet on the fridge: 135, rest, slice. She set the probe, and by quarter to six the number climbed the way numbers climb near the end, slowly, then all at once, and at 135 she pulled the roast out, triumphant, and set it on the board, and texted her father that everything was ready.

Jaida was watching a video on her phone with one earbud in. "Clara," she said. "What did you search last night?"

"Target temperature for pork roast. Why?"

"Search carryover cooking."

Clara searched it. She read the screen, and then she read it again, and then she put the phone face down on the counter and looked at the roast, which was still radiating heat, still working, still cooking itself without her. Carryover cooking meant food kept cooking after it left the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature could rise by several degrees while it rested. She had taken it out at the number. The number had not been the end of anything.

"So it's overcooked," Ziyad said.

"It might be overcooked. Several degrees. Depending."

"Depending on what?"

"Things I can't see from here."

Her father's car was in the driveway. Her mother's was not yet, which gave her twenty minutes, and Clara stood at the board with the knife in her hand and did not cut, because cutting would release what moisture was left, and waiting would keep cooking it further, and both of her choices were real and neither was free. Jaida said, "If it's dry, you make a sauce. You have honey. You have mustard." Ziyad said, "Or you tell them. They'd think it was charming." Clara said, "They'd think it was charming and then they'd eat dry pork on their anniversary," and neither of them argued, because they were her friends and they knew the difference between comfort and help.

She made the sauce. She sliced at five past six, the moment her mother's key turned, and the inside was pinker at the center than at the edges, which meant something, though she would not know exactly what until her parents tasted it and she watched their faces do the thing faces do when people decide how much truth a cook can carry. Her mother said, "You made the honey mustard," and Clara said, "You never said honey mustard," and her mother said, "I didn't. That part's yours," and took a second piece, which Clara decided to count as evidence, knowing it might only be kindness.

She served the potatoes, poured the sparkling water Jaida had gone back out for, and sat down at the table she had set for four with her friends in the kitchen behind her eating off the cutting board. Her father raised his glass. "To sixteen years," he said, and her mother said, "To whoever cooked this," and Clara lifted her glass too.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
The essay was due at midnight, and by four o'clock Alexa had written the same paragraph three times and deleted it twice. She spread the two articles across the little table by the window, hoping the cafe's noise would drown out her own head. One article, by a researcher named Hollis, claimed that later school start times improved adolescent grades across the board. The other, by a pair of economists, found almost no effect at all. Ms. Wanjiru had assigned exactly this: a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, due before the term ended, worth a third of the grade.

The trouble was that Alexa could not find the flaw in either one. Hollis had a tidy study with real students and real transcripts. The economists had a much larger sample, drawn from whole districts, and a colder, more careful voice. When she tried to argue that one was right, she heard the other whispering its objections. Her drafts kept dissolving into "on the other hand," which Ms. Wanjiru had crossed out in red on her last paper with the note, this is not a position, it is a shrug.

Chanel arrived at half four, ordered something with syrup in it, and dropped into the chair opposite without taking off her coat. She was garrulous in the way of someone avoiding her own deadline, and for ten minutes Alexa let herself be carried along by a story about Chanel's brother and a parking dispute, nodding at intervals, her thumb still resting on the page where Hollis reported his effect sizes. Then Chanel noticed the articles and asked what any of it meant.

"They looked at the same question and got different answers," Alexa said. "And I'm supposed to say which one to trust. But I don't know."

"So pick the bigger one," Chanel said, as though it were obvious. "More people, more true."

Alexa almost said that out loud, almost wrote it, and then felt the wrongness of it settle in her stomach. She had spent the whole weekend trying to weigh the two papers against each other, like a judge with two witnesses, when maybe the problem was that she was standing in the wrong courtroom. Bigger was not the same as truer; one noisy study of thousands could mislead more thoroughly than a small careful one. She picked up her phone.

Trenton was at the counter waiting for a coffee, because the universe had arranged itself that way, final exams scattering everyone into the same few warm rooms. He was the one person she knew who read methodology sections for fun, with an asceticism that Alexa privately found excessive, no music, no snacks, just the paper and a pencil. She waved him over and showed him the two abstracts.

"This is my whole problem," she said. "Different studies, same question, opposite answers. There has to be something that looks at all the studies at once. Does that exist, or did I invent it?"

"You didn't invent it," Trenton said. "It's called a meta-analysis." He pulled out his laptop before his coffee had even cooled, and typed with the concentration of someone who had been waiting all term for someone to ask. Within a few minutes he had found one: a paper that had pooled the results of every study on school start times the search turned up, dozens of them, and estimated the overall effect. It came out small. Not nothing, the way the economists had all but claimed, and not transformative, the way Hollis's confident tone had implied. Somewhere in the middle, thin and real.

Alexa copied the citation into her notes and then sat looking at it. The small effect did not settle her essay; it complicated it further. Hollis had probably captured a real improvement but overstated its reach, and the economists had probably rounded something real down toward zero because their data was too coarse to see it. That was a position, she realized, not a shrug. She could hold both articles up against the pooled estimate and say where each one bent away from it, and she could admit, in plain sentences, that the pooling itself depended on which studies had been found and included, which was a limitation she could name but not fix.

"It's due at midnight," Chanel said, checking the time with theatrical despair, as if the deadline were hers.

"Then I need the table," Alexa said, and Chanel gathered her coat and her syrupy cup and moved one table over, close enough to keep talking, far enough that Alexa could not pretend to listen. Alexa opened a blank document and began, for the fourth time, to write the paragraph that had defeated her all weekend. This time the sentences came out in order. She wrote that Hollis and his critics were not opposites but two hands on the same instrument, neither holding it quite level, and that the evidence taken together suggested something modest that both had flattened in opposite directions.

At eleven Ms. Wanjiru came in for a takeaway tea, recognized Alexa, and paused at the table long enough to read the first line upside down. "You found something," she said, in the tone of someone who already knew what it was. Alexa said she had found a way to stand between the two articles without pretending either was worthless, and that she was honest about the parts that stayed uncertain, and that this honesty had cost her the pleasure of being sure. Ms. Wanjiru paid for her tea and did not smile exactly, but something around her eyes gave in.

Alexa submitted at eleven forty, six paragraphs she mostly believed, and closed the laptop on a small ache she could not have named in high school: the gain of a held position, paid for in the loss of the person who could have picked a side and slept easily. Chanel came back over and put her cold cup down next to Alexa's.

"So which article won?" Chanel asked.

"Neither," Alexa said. "That was the point."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.
story:
The blood pressure machine at Ferris Pharmacy sat between the diabetes shakes and the reading glasses, a gray plastic throne with a cuff like a stubby arm, and Madeline had decided it was going to tell her the truth. Her father had come home from his physical with a slip of paper he'd folded twice and put in his shirt pocket, where she'd found it while doing laundry, unfolded it, and understood nothing except the number 118 and the smaller number 76 and the word "borderline" in her own handwriting's imagined voice, which was not actually on the paper at all.

"That thing eviscerated my dignity last Tuesday," said Jean-Felix, who was stocking antacids two aisles over. He had a shift there and a shift at the grocery and somehow still showed up to summer physics review looking like a person who slept. "It squeezed my arm and then printed, like it was doing me a favor. I got 112 over 74 and felt like I'd passed a test nobody told me I was taking."

"Then you passed," Madeline said, rolling up her sleeve. "What's passing?"

"That's the quagmire." He set down the antacids with ceremony. "Nobody at the counter agrees. The pharmacist says one thing, the internet says another, and the machine itself just says thank you for using this device." He did the robot voice of the machine, flat and serene, and a woman reaching for laxatives pretended very hard not to laugh.

Madeline slid her arm into the cuff anyway. It tightened in slow swallows, then released, and the screen blinked up numbers she wrote on the back of a receipt: 116 over 73. Close to her father's. Close to whatever the edge of something was. She stood there holding the receipt like it was evidence in a case she hadn't filed yet, and Jean-Felix leaned on the shelf and watched her think, which he'd learned to do without narrating.

Ms. Chea, the pharmacist, came around the counter with a box of lancets and a look that suggested she had heard the robot voice from three aisles away. Madeline expected to be shooed off the throne, but Ms. Chea only glanced at the screen, still glowing with Madeline's numbers, and raised an eyebrow at the receipt.

"I'm trying to figure out if 118 over 76 is good," Madeline said. "For my dad. The doctor didn't explain, or he didn't listen, which is the same thing with him."

Ms. Chea set down the lancets. She did not launch into a lecture, which Madeline had braced for. She tapped the edge of the machine once and said, "What guide are you using?" and then waited, the way she apparently waited on customers deciding between two antihistamines, as if the deciding were the actual work and not the obstacle to it.

"None," Madeline admitted. "I have a receipt and a hunch."

So Ms. Chea pointed her at the shelf where the store kept its pamphlets, a vestigial rack of glossy paper that everyone walked past, and Madeline dug through gluten-free diets and flu shots until she found the one on blood pressure. She read it standing in the aisle, then read the fine print on the back, where the guidelines were named and laid out, the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association, 2017, and there it was: normal adult blood pressure meant below 120 systolic, the top number, and below 80 diastolic, the bottom one. Both numbers, both under. She read it twice because it felt almost too clean, a line drawn in a place where she'd assumed everything would be fuzzy.

"Okay," she said out loud, holding the pamphlet up like a verdict. "Normal is under 120 systolic and under 80 diastolic. So 118 over 76 is normal. Both numbers are under the line."

"Your dad passed," Jean-Felix said. "Somebody text him."

But Madeline was already frowning at the pamphlet, turning it over, because a single reading felt like a photograph of a river and her father drank cold brew at nine at night and hadn't been to the gym since the gym had a different name. The pamphlet talked about salt and walking and vegetables in the vague cheerleader tone of all pamphlets, no numbers she could hold onto, and one reading on one Tuesday was one reading. Her father's 118 could be his average or his best day. She didn't know. She could say "normal" and be honest, and she could also say "I don't actually know what tomorrow's is," and both of those were true at once, which physics review had not prepared her for.

She bought the pamphlet's advice in the form of a bag of unsalted almonds she suspected her father would eviscerate within a week, meaning the bag, not the almonds, and Jean-Felix rang her up on his register. He held the almonds aloft like a trophy.

"Prescription: beige nuts," he announced. "Take two and call me in the morning."

"Take your own blood pressure first," Madeline said, and swiped her card.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
story:
Mr. Thompson had given him a clipboard and a gymnasium, and David stood at the edge of the stage with the November light going crepuscular through the high windows, feeling that both were inadequate tools. The one-act was due in nine days. He had read the script eleven times, made margin notes in three colors, and rehearsed once, badly, before the basketball team reclaimed the gym and pushed them into the empty cafeteria. Now the actors waited for him in a half circle of folding chairs, and he understood for the first time that directing was not knowing the play but making other people know it.

"From the top of the second scene," he said, and tapped his pencil against the clipboard like a man who believed in it.

Mederic played the brother, the largest part, and he played it with the volume of someone who had never needed a microphone in his life. Rose played the neighbor, four speeches, and she had underlined them all in pencil so lightly it looked like doubt. Her want was quiet but total: she wanted Mederic's scenes to be good, and she wanted one of them to be hers. She had asked David, once, after rehearsal, whether he could move her closer to the argument in the second scene, and he had said maybe, and then spent two nights not deciding.

The second scene began. Mederic crossed from the tables to the counter, delivering the line about the letter, and each time he crossed, Rose, planted near the window, vanished behind him. Not metaphorically. He walked his diagonal and his shoulders closed her off from the imaginary audience, and the audience in this case was a real one: Mr. Thompson, sitting in the fifth row with a legal pad, writing something every time it happened.

"Cut," David said, though no one had used that word with him and he felt like a thief of it. "Mederic, can you take the long way?"

"The long way is boring," Mederic said. "The crossing is the whole point. I'm going somewhere."

"That's the problem. You're going somewhere Rose used to be."

They ran it again. Same result. David's notes had become a kind of private rectitude, rules copied from a library book about stagecraft, rules he enforced without understanding, and it shamed him a little to watch the actors obey them. He was eighteen and giving orders. The gap between his authority and his knowledge felt like a room he could fall into.

It was Rose who solved half of it, though she didn't know she had. On the fifth run she shifted, almost imperceptibly, when Mederic crossed, drifting two steps to her left so that the two of them ended up balanced, one on each side of the stage, both facing front. David stopped the scene. "Do that again," he said. "That thing you just did." She looked frightened, as if caught. "I was just trying to stay visible," she said. He turned the clipboard over and wrote on the back of a permission slip, then looked at Mr. Thompson, who had set down his pen and was watching with something that was not quite permission and not quite refusal.

David walked the cross himself, from table to counter, and saw it plainly at last: when one actor crosses, the other can shift to counter the move, rebalancing the stage so both stay visible to the audience. It was not a rule against movement; it was movement answering movement. He had spent three days treating blocking as a matter of keeping people still, and it was the opposite, a conversation of positions. "When he crosses," David said to the room, "the other person counters. That's what it's called. Countering." Mederic grinned at Rose. "So I get to move and she gets to move." "You get to move because she moves," David said, and heard how much of directing was saying the true thing once, badly, and hoping.

They ran the scene until nine, and by the last pass Rose's shift had become part of her, an answer with her body to Mederic's crossing, and her fourth speech, delivered from the rebalanced stage, landed in the middle of the room instead of off to the side. Afterward Mr. Thompson collected his legal pad and said only, "Tuesday, same time," which David understood to be praise. He helped Rose stack the chairs, and Mederic held the door, and the hallway outside was dark except for one exit sign. Whether the play would be any good he still could not say; nine days was a short time and he was learning the craft the way you learn to swim, by being in over your depth and moving anyway. Rose pulled her coat on and asked, "Same blocking tomorrow?" and David said, "Same blocking, better everything else," and switched off the last light.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same.
story:
Ms. Munro had pushed the desks into a circle, and the rain on the windows made the room feel smaller than it was, which Madeline thought was either a problem or a help depending on whether anyone would actually say anything. The seminar topic was written on the board in her looping hand: Should students be graded on participation? Charles-Olivier had argued no for ten minutes, and he was good at it, the way he was good at everything, restless and mercurial, one minute slouched and bored and the next leaning forward with both hands on the desk like a lawyer in a film.

Madeline had been transcribing the arguments in the back of her notebook, not because she had to but because she wanted to see the shape of them. If we grade participation, she wrote, quiet students are penalized for temperament, not learning. Below it: If we don't, students who coast on written work never learn to think aloud. She liked having both columns. It made her feel like she was holding the question instead of being held by it.

Then Isabelle spoke. "So you're saying we should just let people sit there and contribute nothing," she said, directing it at Charles-Olivier, "and get the same credit as people who actually show up and try."

Madeline looked up from her notebook. She flipped back a page. Charles-Olivier had said, twice, that he wasn't against participation being encouraged, only against it being graded, that a number attached to speaking turned conversation into performance. She read her own transcription again to be sure.

"That's not what I said," Charles-Olivier said, but he said it the way he said most things, half a smile in it, as if being misread were a compliment.

"It's basically what you said." Isabelle had gone pink, which Madeline knew meant she was committed now, that backing up would cost her something in front of twenty-two people and a teacher taking notes by the window.

Madeline's heart did the thing it did before she spoke, a small collapse and rebuild. "Can I read something back?" she said, and Ms. Munro nodded, and Madeline read her notes, the actual sentences, Charles-Olivier's actual position, in her own flat reading voice. "He said grading participation turns speaking into performance. He didn't say anyone should contribute nothing. Isabelle answered a different argument, and then kind of acted like it was the same one."

There was a pause, the particular kind that happens when a room recalibrates. Ms. Munro's pen stopped. "There's a name for that," she said, and Madeline, who had found the term at two in the morning three weeks ago, trying to understand why an online argument had made her feel insane, said it before the teacher could. "A straw man. Attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the one they made, while acting like the two are the same." She felt the words land and immediately wanted half of them back, because Isabelle was looking at her with an expression Madeline recognized: the look of someone deciding whether you are a person or a weapon.

"I wasn't doing it on purpose," Isabelle said, quieter.

"I know," Madeline said, and she did know, mostly. She had done it herself, to her mother, about the dishes, about the curfew, taking the dumbest possible version of a rule and demolishing it and feeling clever. That was the part she hadn't said out loud and wasn't going to: the fallacy wasn't a monster other people committed. It was what happened when you were in a hurry, or tired, or wanted to win more than you wanted to be right.

The discussion moved on, or seemed to. Charles-Olivier started building a hypothetical about a student who never speaks but writes brilliant essays, and someone else proposed a compromise where participation counted only if a student improved over the term, and someone else said improvement couldn't be measured fairly, and Madeline wrote it all down: if X, then Y; if Y, then Z; but Z contradicts the thing we said we valued at the start. She could see the whole structure now, the way conditions stacked and branched, the way every position contained a smaller position it could be flattened into. She offered a synthesis, hesitantly, that maybe grading could exist with an amnesty clause for the first month, a period where silence carried no penalty while students learned the room. Half the circle liked it. Charles-Olivier didn't, and said so, but this time he answered the thing she had actually proposed, and she counted that as a kind of gift, though she couldn't have said to whom.

Afterward, packing up, Isabelle came past her desk. She didn't stop, exactly; she slowed, buckling her bag with unnecessary attention. "Next time just tell me privately," she said. "You didn't have to do it in front of everyone."

Madeline zipped her own bag. She had thought she was being careful, reading from notes instead of accusing, giving Isabelle the out of not doing it on purpose. She saw now that being right in front of other people was its own kind of cost, one her two-column notebook hadn't predicted. There was probably a way to do this that spared everyone, and she hadn't found it, and maybe it didn't exist.

"You're right," she said. "I could have." She didn't say and I'd do it again, and she didn't say and I wouldn't, because she genuinely didn't know yet, and the bell was ringing, and Isabelle was already at the door.

"Tuesday," Isabelle said from the doorway, not turning around, and Madeline stood there holding her notebook, deciding later what to transcribe of that.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Monet showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month.
story:
Amy counted her sketchbooks twice on the bench outside the gallery, as if the number might change. Ten artworks around one theme, that was the assignment, plus an artist's statement, and so far she had eleven paintings of the river behind her grandmother's house that had nothing to do with each other except water.

Inside, Mr. Ahmed was unlocking the small back room where the advanced students would hang their portfolios in June. He nodded at her sketchbooks but said nothing, which Amy took as either kindness or a verdict. Lilly was already there, taping a study of her brother's hands to the wall, and behind her Maelie sat cross-legged on the floor with a catalogue open on her knees.

"You look like someone stole your theme," Lilly said.

"I don't have a theme. I have eleven pictures of a river and a teacher who keeps asking what they're about."

"Then look at this," Maelie said, and turned the catalogue around. It was the gallery's permanent collection binder, and the page she'd found showed a photograph of a room hung edge to edge with paintings of the same field, the same lumps of straw, in different light. "Monet's Haystacks. He showed fifteen paintings from the series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most of them sold within a month."

"Fifteen paintings of haystacks," Amy said. "And people bought them."
