"Most sold within a month. While they were still on the wall."

Amy sat down beside her, careful not to crease the page. She had always thought of a series as a kind of failure of imagination, the artist stigmatized, in her own private vocabulary, as someone who couldn't think of a second idea. Monet apparently thought of one idea and then refused to let it go. She tried to hold both of those in her head at once and found they didn't fit together, which was maybe the point.

"That's not proof of anything," she said anyway. "Buyers in 1891 aren't jurors in June."

"Obviously," Maelie said. "I just like looking at them." She slid the binder closer so Amy could see the reproductions properly, and Lilly came over too, and for a while the three of them just looked: the same stack at dawn, at dusk, in snow, in that pink light that made the straw look like it was burning quietly.

"It's the same painting fifteen times," Lilly said, "except it isn't at all."

Amy opened her first sketchbook. The river in February, gray and clotted. The river in April, high and yellow-brown with melt. The river the evening her grandmother stood on the bank and said the water was lower every year, and Amy had painted it fast, before the light went, without thinking about whether it matched anything. She turned pages and the pages argued with each other, and slowly she stopped seeing eleven failed paintings and started seeing one subject being interrogated.

"I've been doing it backwards," she said. "I kept trying to pick a theme and then make pictures to fit it. But the theme was already there. I just hadn't looked at my own work long enough to see it."

"That sounds suspiciously like epistemology," Maelie said. "How do you know what you know. You know your river by painting it and then reading the paintings."

"Don't make it sound like homework," Amy said, but she was laughing, and Lilly pulled a pencil from behind her ear and held it out like a relay baton.

"Artist's statement," Lilly said. "Start with one sentence and I'll hold you to it."

Amy wrote, crossed it out, wrote again. "The river is changing, and I am learning to look at one thing for a long time." She read it aloud and hated the second half, which sounded like a fortune cookie. "The Monet thing helped, though. If people wanted fifteen haystacks, maybe ten rivers isn't crazy. Maybe a set of pictures of the same subject is the whole point."

Mr. Ahmed had come back into the room without any of them noticing. He looked at the row of Lilly's hand studies, then at the open binder on the floor, then at Amy's sketchbooks.

"Durand-Ruel took a risk on that show," he said. "Nobody had asked collectors to buy the same view over and over." He said it to the wall more than to her, and then he picked up one of her sketchbooks and paged through it without comment, which was apparently how he said most things.

She didn't tell him the part she was still unsure about, which was whether repetition was devotion or just stubbornness, whether her grandmother's disappearing river deserved ten paintings or whether ten was a number she'd chosen because the assignment required it. Maybe by June she'd know. Maybe the statement would have to admit what she didn't.

Lilly taped a fresh sheet to the wall. "Okay. So which ten?"

Amy laid the sketchbooks open across the floor like cards, moved the February river beside the pink evening one, and crouched there, deciding.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the tabling method, melted chocolate is spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming.
story:
Caleb had carried the marble slab for two miles in his backpack, wrapped in a towel, and by the time he reached the campsite his shoulders ached and his opinion of his own plan had soured. The slab belonged to his grandmother, who had used it for nothing he knew of, and he had taken it without asking because asking would have meant explaining, and explaining would have meant hearing himself say that a boy who failed his cooking module wanted to enter the county fair's chocolate division in September.

Kaya was already at the fire pit, boots off, filleting the argument she and Natalie had been having since the drive up. Natalie thought the whole trip was a pretext, which it was, though Caleb preferred to think of it as an intention. He set the slab in the shade of the picnic table and took out the chocolate he had melted at home in a double boiler and carried in a warmed thermos, a trick he had read about and half trusted.

"You're going to make candy at a campsite," Kaya said. "There's no fridge, no tap, no anything. My uncle tried fudge on a trip once and we ate it with spoons out of the pot."

"It's not candy. It has to set shiny and snap. If I just let it cool it goes dull and bends."

"So bring a pot of chocolate that sets dull and bends." She said it lightly, but Caleb heard the ledger under it, the accounting of effort against probable embarrassment, and he understood the arithmetic. He had done it himself in the truck. It was not specious reasoning; it was, by any honest measure, correct. He had never tempered chocolate. He had a camping stove, a creek, and a rock.

Natalie, meanwhile, had been reading. She had printed pages at the library because her phone got no signal out here, and she read them aloud in the flat voice she reserved for information she found absurd. In the tabling method, melted chocolate is spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming. She looked up. "Tabling. That's the word it uses. That's why you brought a slab."

Caleb poured a puddle of chocolate onto the marble, which he had cooled in the creek and dried, and began working it with a palette knife and a bench scraper, spreading it thin and gathering it back, spreading and gathering. The chocolate moved differently as it cooled, thickening, losing its loose solvency, beginning to hold a shape. He could feel something happening through the scraper that he could not have named from the printed page, a gathering intent in the liquid, and he kept his eyes on it because if he looked up he would have to introspect, and he did not want to yet.

"It's going to seize," Kaya said, standing over him now despite herself. "You're overworking it."

"I'm not." But his voice asked rather than answered. He had no grounds for confidence, only a rhythm, spread and gather, and the page in Natalie's hand, and the observation that the chocolate had stopped looking like something that would bend.

They needed a way to know. Mr. Kaur, who kept the camp store two sites down and had come over because he smelled chocolate on the woodsmoke, crouched by the table and said nothing for a while, which Caleb found more bearable than advice would have been. Then Natalie had the idea: the fair entries were judged partly on snap, so test the snap. Caleb smeared a thin coat of the worked chocolate onto the back of a metal spoon and set the spoon in the creek shallows, and the three of them and Mr. Kaur stood at the bank like people waiting for a fish.

The chocolate on the spoon set in less than a minute, and when Caleb flexed the spoon the coating broke with a sound like a knuckle, clean, and the broken edge caught the late light with a hard shine. Nobody spoke. Kaya picked up a fragment and turned it in her fingers and put it in her mouth, and Caleb watched her decide, in real time, that the argument she had been carrying since the trailhead was over. "Okay," she said. "Okay. Do it again and I'll time the creek part."

He did it again. The second batch went onto the slab smoother than the first because his hands had learned something his head had not, spread and gather, and when it thickened he seeded the pot with a spoonful of the tempered chocolate the way Natalie's pages suggested, in a gentler voice than the pages about tabling, and stirred. Some of it still might go wrong. He had no thermometer, no scale, no real certainty that what he had done once he could do twice; the September judges might still bend his chocolate like taffy and write "dull" on a card. But the spoon had snapped, and the fire was drawing down toward the hour when they would eat, and Mr. Kaur had gone back to his store and returned with a square of clean waxed paper.

"Practice for September," Natalie said, and held out the paper.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: In countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration.
story:
The turnoff sign said the university was eleven miles ahead, and Cameron had forty minutes to understand something he had been pretending to understand for two weeks. Noah drove, because Noah's mother had lent them the car on the condition that Noah never let Cameron near the wheel after the parking meter incident, and Graysen rode in the back with the atlas spread across her knees like a general planning an invasion. The regional final was at two o'clock. Cameron's population pyramid, printed at home and left on the kitchen counter beside his lunch, which he had also left there, was not coming.

"Draw it again," Graysen said. "You've drawn it before."

"Drawing it isn't the problem." He flipped open his notebook to the blank page he'd been staring at since the highway. "The problem is what it means. Japan's pyramid looks like a top-heavy Christmas tree, Nigeria's looks like, I don't know, an actual pyramid, and I'm supposed to say what each country needs to build. Schools or nursing homes. That's the whole question. Mr. Choi says the round three questions are always applied."

"Applied means you have to actually decide," Noah said from the driver's seat, and then, quieter, "which is why I got knocked out in round two last year."

Cameron sketched the wide base, the narrowing tower. Nigeria: young, getting younger. Build schools. That one felt obvious, almost cheating. Then he drew the Christmas tree, the bulge in the middle, the thin base at the bottom, and his pencil stopped. The base was thin, but it wasn't nothing. How thin did thin have to be before the population shrank? How would he even operationalize decline, turn a shape on paper into a number that told him the future? He said as much out loud, and Graysen leaned forward between the seats.

"You're overcomplicating it. My cousin did this competition. She said the thing everyone misses is replacement. Two kids per family, one for each parent. Everyone thinks two is the magic number because two people make two people."

"Two people make two people," Cameron repeated. "That's just arithmetic."

"Except it's not the magic number," Graysen said. "She told me it's 2.1. In countries where hardly anyone dies young, the total fertility rate needs to be about 2.1 children per woman to replace the population, if there's no migration. Anything below that, and you shrink. Even 2.0 shrinks you, slowly."

Cameron wrote 2.1 in the margin and circled it. The pencil dug hard enough to dent the next page. So the thin base wasn't just a shape; it was a measurement, a line the country had crossed without knowing it had crossed anything. Two children per family, the number everyone called sensible, the number his own mother mentioned at dinner with a certain satisfaction, was actually a number that emptied schools. And nobody felt it happening, because pyramids change on the scale of decades. It was like homeostasis running in reverse, a body that keeps readjusting itself around a slow loss until the loss is the new normal.

"That's why the Christmas tree keeps pinching in at the bottom," he said. "The base isn't just small. It's below the line."

"Below what line?" Noah asked.

"Two point one."

"Okay," Noah said, in the tone of someone agreeing to a thing he would like explained later, and took the exit.

The parking garage was half empty and smelled of cold concrete. They had twenty-two minutes. Cameron sat on a concrete pillar with the notebook on his knee and built the answer he should have built at home. If the fertility rate sits below 2.1 and stays there, the working-age band thins while the top bands fatten, and within a generation the question is not schools but care, nurses, wards, the whole architecture of an aging population. But the data was equivocal on one point: a rate of 2.1 itself didn't tell him whether it was rising or falling, and a country at 2.1 and climbing needed different plans than a country at 2.1 and sinking. He would have to say that in his answer. He would have to say, in front of judges, that the number told him the present and only gestured at the future.

"That's not a weakness," Graysen said, reading over his shoulder. "That's what she said won her the round. Saying what you can't know."

Inside, the lecture hall smelled like overheated radiators and someone's instant noodles. Mr. Choi was already there, standing at the back with a thermos, and he raised two fingers at Cameron, not quite a wave. Cameron slid into the second row and uncapped his pen. The moderator stepped to the microphone and said the finals would begin in five minutes, and Cameron looked down at his circled 2.1, at the lopsided pyramid beside it, and kept writing.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
Jayden had been hiding the article under his workbook for ten minutes, decoding the final paragraph first because the words there were shorter. Ms. Bouchard's classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and the radiator's dusty heat, and the clock above the door gave him twelve more minutes before she would call someone to stand and summarise the piece aloud, in French, without notes. He knew the strategy was wrong in some vague way he couldn't name, the way he knew he'd parked his bike badly without being able to say how. The last paragraph talked about a mayor's spokeswoman and a petition and something about spring, and none of it seemed to matter.

Miley leaned across the aisle, her pen tapping his sleeve. "What did you get for the first question?"

"I haven't read the first paragraph," he admitted.

"You started at the end?" She said it quietly, as if reporting a small crime. "Our journalism unit in English, remember? Most news articles use the inverted pyramid. The important facts come first, then details after, so the opening paragraph basically carries the whole story." She shrugged. "I skim top down now. Even in French."

Jayden turned back to page fourteen. The article was about a town council in a place called Carcassonne that had voted to restrict a demonstration. He began at the beginning instead, and the sentences opened like doors he'd been pushing on the hinges of. A rally planned for Saturday, a ban approved Tuesday, the reason stated plainly in the second sentence, the names and dates arranged with an almost arrogant confidence that everything he needed was right there, at the top, waiting. The final paragraph, the one he had spent ten minutes dismantling, turned out to be about the weather, the diurnal rhythm of protest planning and the mild forecast that officials hoped would keep crowds small. He had been translating clouds while the mountain sat unread behind his thumb.

"Jayden," said Ms. Bouchard. "Would you like to begin?"

He stood. His mouth went dry in the particular way it did when a room's attention circumscribed him completely, every face drawing a boundary around his voice. He summarised the ban, the vote, the planned rally, and when a detail escaped him, he let it go and reached back for the core of the story the way Miley had said, top down, and it held. His accent wobbled on "manifestation" and he heard Emery, in the back row, murmur the correction under his breath, not unkindly.

"Bon," said Ms. Bouchard. "You gave us the essential facts. Most of you read the article like a novel, beginning to end, and you drown in the third paragraph. Jayden read it like a journalist."

Later, walking to the bus with Miley, he kept turning it over. The article had mentioned a local figure who'd built his following by denouncing the council, a man Miley's dictionary app defined, when she looked it up on the curb, as a demagogue. That word had made the story seem bigger than Carcassonne, bigger than one Saturday and one square. Jayden thought of his grandfather, who read two newspapers every morning, front page first, and who used to say the second cup of coffee was for the details. He'd always assumed that was just an old man's habit, a diurnal ritual like the pigeons outside the kitchen window. Now it looked like a method, something his grandfather had known and never taught because he assumed everyone did it.

"It's weird," Jayden said, "that the writers decide what's most important. The pyramid is their call, not mine."

"Unless you decide the weather paragraph is the real story," Miley said. "Maybe the important facts aren't always the important facts."

He considered that. A ban was a fact; the hope for rain was also a fact, softer, harder to prove, but maybe closer to what people in the town actually felt. He didn't have an answer, and he found he liked that, liked holding the two ideas at once without needing one to collapse into the other.

At home he tried it on an English news story about his own city, reading only the first paragraph and guessing the rest, then checking. He was right about the budget vote and wrong about the school closing, which the paper had buried near the bottom for reasons he couldn't figure out at all. He read the last paragraph twice, out loud, listening to himself, then folded the paper in half and set it under the fruit bowl where his grandfather would find it in the morning.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Each feature in a GIS layer links to a row in an attribute table, so data such as the number of residents in each building can be totaled for a selected area.
story:
The trail climbed out of the parking lot through pines still dripping from the morning's rain, and Alexia kept one hand on her phone where the cached map glowed weakly against her palm. Ms. Sokolov had said the ridge would have signal, which was the whole reason for the hike, but the sky to the west had begun to adumbrate something heavier than weather, a bruise-colored shelf of cloud that the trees kept hiding and revealing as if it were following them.

"The town meeting's Thursday," Marco said, two switchbacks ahead, not even breathing hard. He was the one who had signed them up for the role-play, the one who wanted the panel of teachers to remember his name when scholarships came around in the spring. "I've got the speech written. Fifteen houses in the flood zone. I'll open with that."

"Fifteen houses," Alexia repeated, and something about the phrase snagged on her the way a shoelace catches on a thorn. She stopped walking. Behind her George, who had come for the donuts Ms. Sokolov had promised at the summit, nearly walked into her backpack.

"You always do this," George said. "You get the face. The worrying face."

The wind came up the slope then, and with it a low sound from the west that wasn't quite thunder, and Ms. Sokolov, twenty feet above them, called down that they should keep moving, that the auxiliary trail they'd passed joined the ridge route in half a kilometer if the weather turned. Her voice stayed even, but she had said if, not when, and Alexia had learned to hear the difference in adults' sentences.

At the overlook Ms. Sokolov let them sit on the flat rocks, and the town lay below them, the river cinched through its middle like a belt pulled too tight. Alexia opened the project on her phone, the layers she had spent two evenings building: the flood risk polygon in pale blue, the housing footprints outlined in black. She pinched and dragged until the two layers sat over the same stretch of riverbank, the houses half-drowned in blue. It looked the way Marco's speech needed it to look. It looked like fifteen houses.

But her finger hovered, because she kept thinking about the hearing the class had watched on video, the one from the real town three counties over, where a woman had stood up and asked the council not how many structures but how many people, and nobody had an answer, and the woman had sat down slowly like someone lowering herself into cold water. Alexia tapped one of the black footprints. A small table opened beside it on the screen. A row. Numbers, names, a column that said residents, and a number in that column that was not one. She tapped the next footprint. Another row. Another number. Each feature on the map, she realized with a feeling like the floor of her stomach dropping away, was attached to its own row in the table, and the rows could be added up, all of them at once, for whatever area she selected.

"Marco," she said. "It's not fifteen houses. Select the flood polygon, sum the residents column." Her voice came out steadier than she expected. Below them the river went on being quiet, which felt like a lie the map had already caught.

Marco took the phone. He looked at the total, and his face did the thing where ambition and arithmetic collided, because a bigger number was a better speech, a better speech was a remembered name, and he was smart enough to know that both of them now knew the real one. "Eighty-three people," he said. "Some of those buildings are apartment blocks. Some of the rows have families in them." He said it quietly, testing how it felt in his mouth against the wind.

The first rain arrived as a scatter of fat drops on the rocks, and Ms. Sokolov stood up and pointed them toward the auxiliary trail, the shorter way down, and George groaned about the donuts, and Marco was still holding the phone. Alexia watched the number on the screen, eighty-three, and thought about Thursday, about whether she would say houses or people, and could not yet say which was braver, and the thunder, when it finally came, was closer than any of them had been listening for. Marco pressed the phone back into her hand as they started down.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Roger Tomlinson led development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s, the first computerized GIS, and is often called the father of GIS.
story:
Laura's laptop sat open on the kitchen table between a bowl of cereal she had stopped eating and her mother's unpaid water bill, which she had slid to one side like an accusation. The software was called QGIS, and for three nights it had defeated her. Tonight she had a shapefile of the city's floodplain loaded, red polygon bleeding across the eastern wards, and a second layer the school had licensed for the semester: every parcel of land, every building, coded by whether it was rental or owner-occupied. Her assignment was due Friday. What she wanted, though she hadn't written this in the project proposal, was to know whether her own street sat inside the red.

Tate had promised to come over at seven, and at seven ten he knocked twice and let himself in, the way he had since they were nine. He dropped his backpack on the counter and leaned over her shoulder.

"That's it? That's the whole city?"

"That's the whole city." She zoomed to the river, to the curl of subdivisions built inside the meander, and turned on the flood layer. The red swallowed the subdivisions whole. Then she switched the parcels to graduated colors, and the subdivisions went dark blue, which meant the lowest quartile of household income. The two layers fit together like a lid on a box.

"Okay, that's grim," Tate said.

She didn't answer, because her mother came through in her work uniform, keys already in hand, and stopped at the table long enough to see the screen. "What's that supposed to be?" Her voice was flat, but not unfriendly.

"School project. Overlaying flood risk and housing." Laura kept her cursor moving.

Her mother looked at the dark blue, then at the red over it, then at Laura, and Laura watched her decide not to say the thing she was clearly thinking, which was that they lived two blocks from the dark blue. "Don't stay up all night," her mother said, and the door closed behind her.

They worked for an hour. Tate caught the mistake she'd been making with the attribute table, joining on the wrong field so the income data had been scrambled, and when she re-ran it the map didn't change much, which bothered her more than if it had. She sat back.

"I wanted it to be wrong," she said.

"You wanted your neighborhood not to be in the flood zone."

"No. I mean yes, but also I wanted the data to be cleaner than it is. The flood layer is the hundred-year event from 2009. The parcels are from last year. So anything built since 2009 shows up as safe when it might not be." She pulled up the metadata and turned the laptop so he could read it.

Tate read it twice. "So what do you do?"

"That's what I'm trying to figure out." She opened a new document and typed a sentence, deleted it, typed another. In her notebook, where she'd been keeping notes for the writeup, she had written the word problematize and then crossed it out, because it sounded like something a textbook would say, and then written it again, because it was the right word: the assignment asked her to map flood risk, and what she was actually doing was undermining her own map, on purpose, in the writeup.

Tate was scrolling the software's help pages, looking for something that would fix the 2009 problem, and there wasn't anything, because the problem wasn't technical. "Who even made this stuff?" he said. "Like, who decided computers should do maps."

She had looked that up on Monday, in the hour she'd spent avoiding the attribute table, and she told him the way you tell someone something you half remember and then go verify. "Roger Tomlinson. He led the development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s. It was the first computerized GIS. They call him the father of GIS."

"Canada? I thought this was, like, a Silicon Valley thing."

"Canada. He's the reason we're sitting here failing at this."

Jayson texted at nine with a screenshot of his own map, which was beautiful, all clean gradients and no caveats, and a message: mine's done, you overthinking yours? She looked at it for a long time. His flood layer was the same 2009 layer. His writeup, he'd told her earlier, was three paragraphs about how the map "revealed environmental injustice," full stop, no uncertainty, no note about what the map couldn't show.

She typed back: yours is prettier. Then she closed the message and kept working.

At eleven, Tate gone, the house quiet, she found the asymptote in her own thinking. She had been adding caveats all night, one limitation per paragraph, and the writeup wasn't converging on a conclusion; it was converging on the admission that she couldn't conclude. The putative boundary of the floodplain was a line drawn from a model of a storm that hadn't happened yet, laid over a city that had changed shape since the model was run, and every honest sentence she wrote moved her closer to a limit she could name but never reach: what the actual risk to actual houses actually was. She could say the flood zone and the rental housing overlapped. She could not say, from this data, what would happen to the people in the blue parcels when the water came, or who would be able to move and who wouldn't, because the map had no layer for that, and neither, she suspected, did anyone's.

She saved the file twice, out of habit. Then she zoomed in until the streets had names, found her own block, and measured the distance from the red polygon's edge to her front door with the software's ruler tool: four hundred meters, give or take the accuracy of a line drawn by a model in 2009.

"Give or take," she said to the empty kitchen, and turned off the laptop.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity can briefly reduce strength and power, so many programs warm up with dynamic movement.
story:
The grass was still wet when Anais carried the whiteboard out to the backyard, propping it against the fence where the ladder usually leaned. She had drawn seven columns, one for each day, and beneath them she wrote the word Tuesday twice before rubbing one out with her thumb. Her season started in three weeks, and her problem was simple: she had never planned anything longer than a single afternoon.

Fabrice arrived first, cutting through the gap in the hedge the way he always did, holding a laminated sheet he'd printed from a coaching forum. Marcel came a few minutes later with a bag of oranges and an opinion about everything, which he began delivering before he had fully passed through the gate. "You're doing it wrong already," he said, pointing at the whiteboard. "You've got hard days next to each other. Legs don't work like that."

"Legs aren't the part I'm stuck on," Anais said. She tapped the corner of the board where she had written, in smaller letters, warm-up? "Before the time trials last month, I held my stretches on the line. The long ones, the kind where you settle into the hamstring stretch and count. I felt flat the whole race. Like my legs were borrowed."

Fabrice sat down on the upturned crate and looked at his sheet. "That tracks," he said slowly. "Holding a static stretch for a long time, like sixty seconds or more per muscle, right before something explosive can briefly reduce your strength and power. It's on here somewhere."

Marcel, who could be loquacious even about oranges, went quiet for a moment, which was how Anais knew it had landed. "So what do people do instead?" he asked.

Fabrice ran his finger down the page. "Dynamic stuff. Leg swings, walking lunges, skips. Movement, not holding."

Anais wrote dynamic across the top of her warm-up column, then stood back and looked at it. Her coach had always told her to stretch out properly, and her mother said the same thing before any run, and both of them had decades of being right about other subjects. It was strange to hold two pictures in her head at once: the old one, where holding a stretch was the responsible thing to do, and this new one, where the same act, timed differently, could take something away from her. She didn't think the old picture was wrong, exactly. It just belonged somewhere else in the day, after the work, or on the rest days she now needed to draw in.

"The thing I can't figure out," she said, "is where the rest days go. If I put them wrong, the whole week collapses."

From the other side of the fence, Mr. Çelik looked up from his tomato stakes. He had been listening, she realized, the way he usually did, without pretending otherwise. "You're overthinking it," he called. "Hard day, easy day, rest day. Even the virtuoso pianists on my street don't practise the same passage full speed all week." He bent back to his twine, which was his way of saying he was finished contributing.

Anais laughed, and then stopped, because something in what he'd said had settled. Full speed every day was not a plan; it was a hope wearing a plan's clothes. She erased her Tuesday, moved the quality session to Thursday, and dropped a rest day on either side of it like a frame around a picture.

Marcel, peeling an orange, watched her work. "You're going to follow this? Actually follow it?"

"I'm going to try to internalize it," she said. "Not just write it. Live it a week and see what my legs tell me." She drew a small box at the bottom of the board and labelled it notes, because she suspected the plan would be wrong in places she couldn't see yet, and she wanted a place to be honest about that when it happened.

By the time the sun moved behind the garage, the board held a whole week: dynamic warm-ups before the fast work, long stretches moved to the evenings, one full day of nothing but walking. Fabrice copied it onto his palm with a pen, smudging it immediately. Marcel ate his third orange and argued for a second rest day, and Anais left it as a question in the notes box rather than an answer, because she did not know yet, and pretending otherwise seemed like a smaller kind of failure than admitting it.

She carried the board to the porch so the dew wouldn't wash it out overnight. From the fence, Mr. Çelik said, "Leg swings tomorrow, then."

"Skips too," she said, and turned off the light.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
The pasta was supposed to take eleven minutes, and at twelve it was still chalky in the centre, so Xavier fished a piece out of the pot with a fork, blew on it, and bit down on something that felt like a promise not yet kept. His father had gone down to the lake with the little ones, and his mother was asleep in the tent with a headache, which meant dinner was his entirely: the pasta, the sauce he was reducing in the smaller pot, the whole careful architecture of the meal. He had planned it for a week, timing everything so the sauce would finish as the noodles drained, and now the noodles were refusing to cooperate.

He turned the little dial on the camp stove, but the flame was already as high as it would go, and the water had settled into a rolling boil that somehow seemed less fierce than the water at home. The campsite sat well up the mountain, high enough that the air felt thin when he climbed the trail to the washrooms, high enough that the arboreal wall of pines around their site had opened into a view of ridgelines stacked behind ridgelines. Something was different up here, he thought, something about the water itself, though he could not have said what.

"You're staring at that pot like it insulted you," said Laetitia, who was sitting on the picnic table with her feet on the bench, watching him with the patience of someone who had run out of things to read. Her family's site was two down from his, and she had attached herself to Xavier's cooking project on the first night, mostly, he suspected, because her own family believed dinner meant granola bars.

"It's not done," Xavier said. "It should be done. It's been forever."

Kaylin appeared from the path with a water bottle and the self-appointed authority of someone who had read the campsite notice board twice. "Ms. Toussaint told my brother the same thing happened to them last summer," she said. "Their potatoes took hours. She said water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude. Like, at five thousand feet it's only about ninety-five degrees Celsius, so boiled food takes longer to cook."

Xavier looked at her, then at the pot, then at the altimeter app on his phone, which read 5,300 feet. Ninety-five degrees. Not quite a hundred, not quite the fierce heat his mother's kitchen produced, and the pasta could not tell the difference between water that looked angry and water that was actually, chemically, gentler. It would just take longer. That was all. He felt something in his chest loosen, the specific relief of a mystery turning into a fact.

"Okay," he said. "So we wait." He covered the pot with the lid to hold what heat there was, and adjusted his timers, pushing the sauce to low so it would not reduce past rescue. The three of them sat around the table while the light dropped through the trees, and he told them about the meal plan he had made at home, the lists, the little drawings of plates. Laetitia said he was the only person she knew who treated spaghetti like a cabinet reshuffle. He laughed, though privately he liked the comparison; he had, after all, planned this dinner partly to show his parents he could be trusted with real responsibility, the way his older sister always was, and a dinner that collapsed would abrogate that whole argument in one evening.

He tried the pasta again at sixteen minutes. Closer. At nineteen, it gave, and he drained it into the colander with steam rising into the cooling air, then folded it into the sauce while Kaylin set the plates on the table without being asked. His father came up the trail with the little ones shouting about frogs, took in the steaming pot, the set table, the smell of garlic in pine-scented air, and put a hand briefly on Xavier's shoulder, which in his father's language was a paragraph.

There was one thing Xavier still did not understand, sitting there while everyone ate and declared it good: whether it was the altitude alone or something he had done besides, whether the noodles at home would behave differently now that he knew to watch for this. He decided he would test it when they got back, same brand, same time, and see. Laetitia leaned over and took seconds without asking, and he pushed the pot toward her across the plank table.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
The gym smelled like rubber mats and cold coffee, and Ryan sat on the bleachers with his phone open to a page he'd found at one in the morning, reading the same paragraph for the fourth time. In her 2017 book Radical Candor, Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly. He'd come to it sideways, through a video Cade had sent him with the caption "you need this more than I do," and Cade wasn't wrong.

The problem had a name, and the name was Noa. They'd been assigned as partners for the robotics qualifier, and Noa built beautiful chassis, clean solder work, wiring like a diagram. But her code was a disaster, and everyone on the team knew it and nobody said it, because Noa cried when she was criticized, or worse, went quiet in a way that made the whole lab feel like a held breath. Last season they'd lost a regional match because her autonomous routine sent the robot into a wall for eleven straight seconds while three people watched and said nothing. Afterward Mr. Aziz had asked, mildly, why nobody had flagged it in testing, and the room had developed a sudden fascination with its shoes.

Ryan walked to the lab after last period carrying the silence of the whole previous year in his chest. Noa was already there, hunched over the laptop, and she looked up with an effusive greeting that made it worse, because she was glad to see him, because she liked him, and that was exactly the thing the book said you were supposed to keep while saying the hard part.

"You want to run the new routine?" he said.

She hit enter. The robot executed a flawless ninety seconds, and Ryan felt a flicker of hope, and then, on the return leg, it drifted four inches off line and clipped the corner of the practice box. Noa made a small sound and reached for the laptop. Ryan reached for it first.

"Can I look at the odometry loop?"

"It's fine. It's just the box."

"It's not just the box." He said it too fast, too flat, and he watched her face close like a door. This was the moment where last year's version of him said "actually, whatever, we'll fix it later," and later meant never, and never meant the wall. He turned the laptop toward himself and scrolled, buying ten seconds. "There's a drift term here that compounds. See, after the turn, you're not resetting the error, so it keeps accumulating."

"That's not how it works," Noa said.

"It is how it works. I watched it happen four times last Tuesday and didn't say anything, and that was on me." The words came out before he'd arranged them, and he heard how they sounded, an accusation shaped like an apology. She stood up. He stood up too, which was a mistake, because now it was two people on their feet in an empty lab.

"You could have said something Tuesday."

"I know."

"So why didn't you?"

He had an answer and it wasn't flattering. "Because it was easier to let you drive into the wall and then feel bad for you than to tell you the code was broken. That's not nice. I read this book called Radical Candor. It says the two things go together, caring about the person and challenging them directly, not one or the other." It came out like reciting, and he hated it, and Noa stared at him with her arms crossed.

"You read a book about how to talk to me?"

The sentence landed wrong, somewhere between insult and absurdity, and Ryan felt the whole approach wobble. He'd thought the idea was a tool, and it turned out it was also a thing you could be excoriated for, weaponized against you by the very person it was supposed to help. "It's not," he started, and stopped, because he'd been about to explain, and Mr. Aziz was always saying that explanations delivered under fire sounded like excuses. Instead he pulled his notebook out of his bag, the one with the Tuesday run logged in it, timestamps and drift measurements he'd taken without telling her, and set it on the bench between them.

Noa looked at the numbers for a long moment. "You measured it."

"Every run."

"That's kind of creepy, Ryan."

"That's also the only reason I know it's the reset and not the sensors." He tapped the page. "You're not bad at this. Your threading is better than mine. But this one thing, it's going to cost us the qualifier, and I'd rather you be furious at me in November than have us both stand there in December watching the robot hug a wall."

She sat down slowly, still holding the notebook, and there was no armistice announced, no moment where the conflict resolved into warm agreement, only the quieter fact of her pulling the laptop back toward herself and scrolling to the loop he'd flagged. She read the code in silence while Ryan put the robot back on the start marker and crouched to check the wheels.

"You could have just led with the notebook," Noa said, not looking up.

"Noted," he said, and set the bot down on the tape.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
The clutch had opinions. Sara had been in the driver's seat of her mother's little manual for eleven minutes, and in that time she had stalled it four times, twice at the same roundabout, which felt like a personal insult from the roundabout itself. Her mother sat in the passenger seat with her hands folded very politely in her lap, the posture of someone pretending not to be terrified.

"Gently on the clutch," her mother said, for the ninth time, in the tone of a woman reciting a prayer she no longer believed in.

"I am being gentle. The car is being obstreperous." Sara turned the key again. The engine caught, snarled, and held. She eased out of the Tesco car park and onto the road, where a van behind them honked with real feeling. "See? Everyone in this town hates me now. I've been maligning myself in public for twenty minutes."

In her pocket, her phone buzzed. She ignored it until they'd survived a left turn, then checked at the lights. Tori, three messages: "how's the lesson," "did you die," "important question." The important question was whether Sara wanted to split a block of automatic lessons at the driving school in town, because Tori's cousin had done automatic and passed in six weeks and, in Tori's words, "basically never cried once."

Sara typed back with one thumb while her mother made a small sound of disapproval. "can't. mum's car is manual. whole point."

"so do automatic," Tori replied. "so much easier."

The lights changed. Sara moved off, stalled, restarted, and thought about it in the gaps between gear changes. It would be easier. Tori wasn't wrong. The automatic would remove the clutch entirely, that pedal that seemed to have a grudge against her, and six weeks from now she'd have a pink licence and freedom. The thought was genuinely tempting, sitting there in third gear, sweat on her palms.

But there was the thing Tori had said last week, at Julien's birthday, when his older brother had driven them all to the chip shop in his rattling manual. Julien's brother had mentioned it offhand, in the way people mention things they've recently learned and can't stop repeating: "Did you know if you pass your test in an automatic, you can only drive automatics? You'd have to pass a whole other test before you can drive a manual." Sara had half listened then, watching Julien steal his brother's chips. In the car now, it came back to her whole.

"Light's green," her mother said.

"I know, I know." She moved off, more smoothly this time, the clutch biting at almost the right moment. She laid it out for her mother in the gaps of concentration. Automatic would be quicker, easier, less weeping. But their family car was manual, and her mother's car was the only car, and a licence that didn't let her drive it was a licence to sit in the passenger seat of her own freedom. She'd be done faster and still have to ask for lifts to everything, forever, until she retook a test she could have taken now.

"So you're doing it the hard way on purpose," her mother said. "You've become a pragmatist. I didn't raise you like this."

"You raised me with one car and it's this one. That's pragmatism by force."

She texted Tori at the next lights, one thumb, fast: "if you pass in an automatic you can only drive automatics. you'd have to pass again for a manual. mum's car is manual. not splitting the block, sorry."

Tori's reply came as they pulled onto their own street, which Sara took slowly, triumphantly, in second gear the whole way like a small stubborn boat. "wait WHAT. nobody TOLD me. julien's brother has a manual. ugh. fine. manual block then. we can cry together."

"You can drive my car," Sara said out loud, to nobody, grinning.

"Whose car?" her mother asked.

"Mine. Apparently." She pulled into the driveway, crooked but moving, and shut off the engine. For a moment neither of them moved. Then her mother reached over and straightened the mirror she'd been gripping secretly with two fingers for the last half mile.

"Same time Thursday," her mother said. "You're buying the tea."

"I'm eighteen and unemployed."

"Then you're making the tea." Sara took the keys, weighed them in her palm, and went in to fill the kettle.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table, and a foreign key in one table, such as an order's customer ID, points to a primary key in another.
story:
Benjamin had told anyone who would listen, including the cashier at the sandwich place near school, that he was fluent in two languages now, English and SQL, and he had told them this with the confidence of a person who had finished exactly one online course. So when Ms. He posted the lab assignment on Thursday, he opened his laptop before she had finished describing it, which was how he missed the description.

The lab was small and local, in the way of all her examples: a database for a nursery in town, two tables, one called customers and one called orders. Find the customers who ordered nothing. Benjamin typed his usual query, joined the tables, ran it, and got a list of eleven customers. He was three lines into a message to Ryker announcing his victory when he counted the customers in the customers table. There were nineteen.

He did not mention the missing eight to Ryker. Instead he sent: "Finished in six minutes. This might honestly be beneath us." Ryker replied with a thumbs up and nothing else, which Benjamin chose to read as deference.

Colby, two seats over, was having a different experience. She had both tables open and was staring at them the way people stare at vending machines that have eaten their money. "I can't even get the join to work," she said. "It says the column names don't match." Benjamin leaned over, magnanimous, because helping Colby cost him nothing and looked good. Her customers table had a column called customer_id. Her orders table also had a column called customer_id. Benjamin looked at that for a while. In his own query he had joined customers.customer_id to orders.customer_id, which was the only thing the names suggested, and it had worked, sort of, the way a screen door works as a door.

"Wait," Colby said, mostly to herself. "This column here, customer_id in the orders table, it's a foreign key. It points at the primary key in customers." She tapped the screen twice. "And the primary key is the one that uniquely identifies each row." She said this the way people recite the one fact they retained from a textbook, then went quiet, and Benjamin felt something rearrange itself in his head. Every order pointed at exactly one customer. Every customer might have no orders pointing at them at all. His join had kept only the customers who had at least one order, which was why they all appeared, cheerful and duplicated, in his results. The eight silent customers had been erased by the join itself, not by bad data. He had built a machine for finding the loud people and then asked it where the quiet people went.

He opened Ryker's chat again and typed a correction, then deleted it, then typed a shorter one, then put his phone face down on the desk. His earlier message sat there in the thread like a signed contract.

Ms. He circulated. She had a way of reading over a student's shoulder without comment, which was worse than comment. Benjamin tried LEFT JOIN, remembered it from the course's fourth week, which he had watched at double speed, and added a condition that the order's ID be null. Nineteen rows came back, then eight after he fixed a typo. Eight customers, names and emails and towns, who had signed up and never spent a dollar.

Colby looked over. "How'd you get all of them?" He started to say he'd known the whole time, and heard himself, and stopped. "I got it wrong first," he said. "I found the opposite of the answer and thought it was the answer." She nodded and copied his query into her own file, which felt, oddly, better than the thumbs up had.

Ms. He paused behind them long enough to read the screen, then said only, "Good," and moved on. Attached to the lab was a district form Benjamin's mother had to sign, some language about how the school would indemnify the nursery against liability for students touching their real data, and Benjamin signed out, printed it, and folded it into his backpack while the room emptied.

That night Ryker sent him a screenshot of his own results, eleven rows, with the caption "done, six minutes." Benjamin looked at it for a long time. He typed "count the customers," and deleted it. He typed "check the total," and deleted that too. Finally he sent the eight names, nothing else, and turned his phone over on the desk, screen down, still lit.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Mark 2:27, Jesus says that the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath, answering critics of his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath.
story:
Nicolas had the folded page in his jacket pocket for the whole walk through the cemetery gates, and by the time they reached the third row of headstones the paper had gone soft at the crease. His mother carried the flowers. His grandmother had been dead since March, and this was the second visit, the first having been too cold to say much of anything.

The headstone was small and gray and said only her name and the years. Beside it, one plot over, an older stone carried a longer inscription, something about a man who had spent forty years on fishing boats, and his family had called his a pelagic life, a life of the open ocean. Nicolas read it twice while his mother knelt and rearranged the flowers that were already fine.

"You're doing homework at a grave," his mother said.

"It's not homework exactly." He took out the page. "Mr. Pérez gave us the debate topic Thursday. Whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life, and you can only argue from the text itself. No outside sources. He picked the Sabbath for me."

"Of course he did."

Mr. Pérez knew about the grandmother. He had been her neighbor for eleven years, and after the funeral he had told Nicolas that arguing with her had been the best training anyone could get. Nicolas was scheduled to argue the affirmative side on Tuesday: that the rule still binds. The problem was that every time he built a case from the commandments and the prophets, a voice in his head answered in his grandmother's exact cadence, and the case fell apart.

He had tried the verse on her once, the spring before she died, when Sunday debate practice had been moved to the morning and she said it was wrong. "The Sabbath was made for man," he had told her, "and not man for the Sabbath. That's Jesus, in Mark, chapter two, verse twenty-seven. He said it when critics attacked his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath." He had been proud of it. He had found it himself.

She had looked at him for a long moment and said, "Then keep it, if you're the kind of man it was made for." That had ended the argument, and he still could not say which of them had won.

His mother stood up and brushed dirt from her knees. "She left you something, you know. The lawyer sent it over last week and I keep forgetting. She called it her deposition, which I thought was dramatic, even for her. It's a letter, signed and dated, about the property line, but the property line part takes up one paragraph. The rest is for you."

Nicolas felt the folded page in his pocket become, suddenly, a lesser document.

"So here's my actual question," he said. "If I argue Tuesday that the rule still applies, I'm arguing against her. And if I quote the verse, I'm quoting a verse she already beat."

"That's not a question," his mother said. "That's a complaint."

Behind them, a car door closed, and Gracie came up the path with two coffees and Brooklynn trailing behind her, still in soccer warmups, which meant they had come straight from the Sunday practice Nicolas had skipped. They had come to watch him lose his mind over the topic, which was a form of entertainment for them.

"He's stuck," his mother said, and kissed his head, and walked back toward the car to give them the graveside, which was a phrase Gracie would repeat for weeks.

Gracie sat on the low stone wall. "Tell us the case."

"The case is that the commandment is unconditional. Six days you labor, the seventh is rest, it doesn't say unless. It delimits the week, it sets a boundary, and a boundary isn't a suggestion. That's the affirmative."

"Okay," said Brooklynn. "Now lose it."

"The counter is the verse I quoted her. Man was not made for the Sabbath. The Sabbath was made for man. Which sounds like the rule serves people, and if it stops serving them it stops binding them. But that can't be the whole answer either, because then any rule dissolves whenever it's inconvenient, and she knew that, and that's what she meant by keep it if you're the kind of man it was made for."

Gracie blew on her coffee. "So argue both."

"That's not a debate, that's a hedge."

"It's a position," Brooklynn said. "Mr. Pérez keeps saying the good debaters aren't the ones with the cleanest case, they're the ones who can hold two things."

Nicolas looked at the headstone with her name on it, and then at the fisherman's stone beside it, forty years on the open water and still ending up here, on a hill, in the ground, in a town two hundred miles from any sea. He took out his phone and typed a single line to himself, the way Mr. Pérez had taught them, the thesis that would delimit the whole round: the rule stands, but it stands as a gift stands, and a gift refused long enough stops being given.

"Still doesn't say what to do about Sunday practice," Gracie said.

"Nothing says what to do about Sunday practice." He put the phone away. "That part stays open."

His mother called from the car and held up an envelope. It was thin, and on the front, in the handwriting he knew better than anyone's alive, it said Nicolas, read it standing up.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021), the Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post.
story:
The marble steps of city hall were still cold at noon, and Jasmine climbed them holding her brief like a plate of food she wasn't sure she wanted to eat. Inside, the council chamber had been rearranged into a courtroom for the day, three municipal judges volunteering as the bench, and Ms. Lombardi was pinning a sign to the railing that said MOCK SUPREME COURT in letters that looked borrowed from a bake sale. Jasmine was petitioner's counsel. Her friend Timothe, drawing the school district's side, was already seated and grinning at her in a way she found peevish, though she had to admit the word was unfair. He had reason to grin. Their case was Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., and everyone in the room knew which side history had chosen.

She had spent two weekends with the actual opinion. The facts were simple enough to recite in her sleep: a student, off campus, on Snapchat, posted something vulgar about her school and her team, and the school punished her for it. In 2021 the Supreme Court ruled eight to one that punishing that off-campus post violated the student's free speech. Eight to one. Jasmine had underlined the tally in two colors, then crossed out one underline because it looked desperate.

The problem was that she didn't believe her own side anymore. Or rather, she believed it and didn't, the way you can believe a friend should be allowed to say something and still wish she hadn't said it. Ms. Lombardi had assigned the sides by lottery, and Jasmine had drawn the student, the girl everyone called B.L., and defending her meant arguing that schools had almost no reach past the parking lot. But Jasmine kept imagining the Snapchat spreading through her own school by third period, and the coach reading it, and the season folding up like a lawn chair.

She argued the first round anyway, and it went well. "The Court held, eight to one, that punishing an off-campus Snapchat post violated her free speech," she told the bench, and one of the judges nodded slowly, the way judges nod when they already know. Timothe cross-examined her on bullying, on threats, on the cases where school authority did extend beyond the gate, and she parried each one because she had made the arguments to herself at two in the morning and lost most of them. Winning in public was easier than winning alone.

The second round was the one that mattered, because Ms. Lombardi had announced a twist that made half the room groan: the finalists would switch sides. Jasmine would defend the school district. Timothe, catching her eye across the aisle, mouthed the word hedonist at her, which made no sense in any legal context but perfectly captured how much he was enjoying himself. During the recess she sat on the wide front steps eating a soft pretzel and trying to build the district's case out of the wreckage of her own. The school had wanted to indemnify itself, she thought, not against lawsuits exactly, but against chaos, against the tide of a screenshot traveling where no teacher could follow it. That word felt wrong even in her head. Schools indemnify against liability. What this one had wanted was control.

From the back of the chamber, Kellen watched Jasmine take the podium for the second time and thought she looked like a different person. Kellen had judged her first round harshly, privately, on a folded piece of paper where she kept score for her own amusement. The first Jasmine had been smooth, confident, a little glib. This one paused. This one stood in front of three judges and said, "I'm going to argue the school's side now, and I want to be honest about what the school can't do." Then she laid it out: the Supreme Court had said the punishment violated the student's speech, eight to one, and the district could not win by pretending otherwise. What the district could do, she argued, was claim the narrow ground the Court had left open, the messy off-campus middle where a school might still act if it could show real disruption, real harm, not just hurt feelings in a hallway.

One of the judges leaned forward. "Counsel, are you conceding the constitutional question?" "I'm conceding the ruling," Jasmine said. "I'm not conceding that the ruling answers every case that comes after it." The room went quiet in the way a room does when someone stops performing and starts thinking out loud, and Kellen stopped keeping score on her paper.

Timothe's rebuttal was sharp, and he won on style, and when the judges conferred they split two to one, which meant nothing and everything. Afterward Ms. Lombardi found Jasmine gathering her papers. "You argued better against yourself than for yourself," she said. "That's usually the sign of someone who'll be a real lawyer. Or a terrible one. I forget which."

Outside, Timothe caught up with her on the steps. "So which side do you actually believe in?" he asked. Jasmine looked at her brief, at the underlines and the crossed-out underline, at the tally she had memorized down to the lone dissenter. "Both," she said. "Ask me again after I post something stupid on a Saturday." She handed him the last bite of her pretzel and walked down toward the bus stop, brief under her arm, arguing quietly with herself all the way.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A margin of error is expressed in percentage points, not percent: plus or minus 3 points on a 58 percent result means a likely range of 55 to 61 percent.
story:
Jordan set his phone face-down beside his plate before his mother could comment on it, but he kept thinking about the draft anyway, the way you keep tonguing a tooth that aches. The school paper's lead story, due to Ms. Yoon by eight o'clock, claimed the senior class favored the later start time, 58 percent in favor, with, as Eugene had written it, a margin of error of 3 percent. Three percent. Jordan had read the sentence four times in fifth period and something about it had snagged, the way a shirt catches on a nail, without tearing all the way through.

"Your father says you're editing now," his mother said, spooning rice into his bowl. "Big man."

"Copy editor," Jordan said. "I fix other people's mistakes."

His father grunted, not unkindly, and asked whether he'd fixed anything good lately. Jordan started to say no, and then stopped, because the sentence was sitting right there behind his teeth. He picked up the phone again, opened the draft, and read it aloud: "Fifty-eight percent support the change, with a margin of error of 3 percent."

"What's a margin of error?" his little brother asked, reaching across for the soy sauce.

His mother told him to eat. Jordan pushed his own food around and tried to cogitate through the problem, which was hard with his brother narrating his day and his father asking whether the team had won. He excused himself from the table, which his mother allowed with a look, and stood in the hallway where he could still hear the clink of dishes.

He did the arithmetic the way he'd done it in fifth period, on his palm with a finger. If the margin were 3 percent of 58 percent, that would be a point and a fraction, practically nothing. But the whole senior class was only 214 people, and the poll had gone out to maybe 80. He remembered Alina laughing at her own ballot, clicking "yes" twice on her laptop because she thought it was funny. He remembered Eugene saying they'd gotten "enough responses," with the confidence of someone who had never once wondered what enough meant. Somewhere between those two memories, the sentence came apart in his hands.

He texted Alina first, because she'd taken statistics. "If the poll says 58 percent and the margin is plus or minus 3 points, what does that actually mean?" She replied fast, with her usual refusal to be pithy when she could be exact: "Points, not percent. It means the real number could be anywhere from 55 to 61." He read it twice. Points. Not percent. Not a sliver of the result, but three whole percentage points on either side of it, a band the truth could wander inside. And Eugene's sentence, if you read it the way any reader would, said the opposite: that the poll was nearly perfect.

He went back to the table and sat down. His father had moved on to complaining about a phone survey, some company calling about the election, and Jordan found himself listening differently than he had a year ago, when he would have repeated whatever number he'd heard as though it were scripture. "They said forty-two percent," his father said, "so that's what people think."

"Could be thirty-nine," Jordan said. "Could be forty-five. Depends on the margin."

His father looked at him, and his mother looked at him, and for a moment the table went quiet. Then his brother said Jordan was weird, and dinner resumed.

At his desk afterward, Jordan opened the draft. He changed "3 percent" to "3 percentage points," and then added the range in Alina's words, 55 to 61, because a reader like his father, or like his brother, deserved the whole truth and not just its most confident shadow. He sat for a while before hitting send. The veracity of the article mattered to him, but so did something harder to name: Eugene had stayed late in the newsroom for three nights running, and Jordan knew how it would land, coming from the copy desk, this small red correction on his best paragraph. He thought about messaging Ms. Yoon instead, letting her catch it, letting the correction come from above. He thought about last fall, when Jordan had written a caption wrong himself and Eugene had fixed it without telling anyone, quietly, before it printed.

He sent the note to Eugene directly. "Good numbers. One fix on the margin. It's points, not percent, so the range is 55 to 61." He set the phone down. The screen lit once, twice, and then went dark. He left it there and went to find the leftover pie.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
Grandpa's living room smelled of cardamom tea gone turbid in its pot, and every seat had been claimed an hour before kickoff, so Mia sat on the arm of the couch with Harleen's legs across her lap like a gate arm. The whole family had driven out for the final, and the TV, older than Mia, made the pitch look mildly radioactive. "That grass is not that colour," Harleen said. "It's in Russia. Maybe it is," said Nora from the floor, where she was being slowly incapacitated by the sleeping dog, a spaniel who had chosen her as furniture.

Ninety minutes of nothing had produced, in order, one disallowed goal, two arguments, and a plate of pastries. In the fourth minute of added time, with everyone half-resigned to extra time, the striker turned and hammered the ball into the roof of the net. The room detonated. Uncle stood on the coffee table. Grandpa, who had been asleep since minute sixty, woke and joined the cheering without asking what had happened, a trick Mia admired more than she could say. Then the referee put his finger to his ear and pointed at the sky, and the stadium screen said CHECKING, and the room went quiet enough that the teapot could be heard ticking.

"No," Harleen said. "No, no. What is he checking? It was clean. I saw it live."

"You saw it once, at full speed, from an angle," Nora said, not lifting her head off the dog. "He's talking to the video people."

Mia had her phone out already, thumbing through the tournament rules she'd half-skimmed weeks ago. "It's called the video assistant referee," she said. "It's new. This is the first World Cup they've used it at, this whole thing in Russia."

"So they can check anything?" Harleen grabbed her ankle. "Anything, any time? Offside by a toenail in minute three?"

"No, that's the part." Mia scrolled, frowning at a wall of text. "Only certain things. Goals, obviously, which is this, and penalties, and direct red cards." She paused, reread, and started laughing. "And mistaken identity. If the ref sends off the wrong player."

"Send off the wrong player," Harleen repeated. "How, by accident?"

"Twins," Nora said solemnly, from the floor. "Or bad eyesight. Or two brothers with the same haircut." Grandpa nodded along as though this were a reasonable feature of modern football, and Mia thought of the story he told every visit, about refereeing village matches on the steppe near where he grew up, dust so fine the lines disappeared and he had to guess, and both teams agreeing to trust him because the alternative was no football at all. She had never quite believed the dust detail. It seemed, now, less exotic than she'd assumed.

On screen, the check went on and on. The striker stood alone with his hands on his hips, and the stadium held its breath with the room. "If they take this back," Uncle said, to nobody, to God, "I'm going outside to look at the garden until it's over." Mia found she was doing something odd with her own loyalty: she wanted the goal to stand for Harleen's sake, and half-hoped it wouldn't, for the pleasure of the argument afterward. Both feelings sat together comfortably, like the dog and Nora, and she made no effort to choose between them.

The screen cut to a drawn line. The replay ran. The whole room leaned toward the screen and saw it at once: the ball had clipped the striker's arm, a small ugly deflection, in the buildup. The referee crossed his arms above his head, and the goal was gone. Harleen made a sound like a kettle. "That's not fair, the handball wasn't what they were checking, they were checking the goal, and then, and then," and Uncle put his coat on inside out and opened the door to the garden, and Grandpa stood, cleared his throat, and produced from the sideboard a brass whistle, green with age.

"I never had a video," he said, holding it up so it caught the light. "But I had this, and two ears." He blew it, sharply, and the dog barked, and from the kitchen, where she had supposedly been ignoring football her entire life, Grandma shouted, "Offside! He was offside! In the second half! Nobody listens to me!" Harleen stared at her, then at Mia, then began, helplessly, to laugh. On the television, unperturbed, the referee pointed to the spot: a penalty. Nora sat up, dislodging the spaniel, and said, "Wait. They can check that too. Mia, tell me they can check that too."

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Albert Mehrabian's often-quoted '7 percent words, 38 percent tone, 55 percent face' rule came from experiments on conveying feelings, and he said it does not apply to all communication.
story:
Aaron's mother had taped the grocery store notice to the refrigerator door, a single sheet about a Saturday clerk position with the phrase "interviews Thursday" underlined twice in her pen. He had pulled out his phone, searched for how to interview well, and fallen down a video rabbit hole until one clip snagged in his mind. A man in a blazer said, with total confidence, that only seven percent of communication was words. Thirty-eight percent was tone and fifty-five percent was face, the man said, tapping his own cheek. Aaron lay on his bed holding the phone above him, doing the arithmetic. If that was true, the words of his answers barely mattered. He could mumble through "Why do you want this job?" and win with eyebrows alone.

He collated what he had into a list on lined paper anyway, because it felt wrong not to: availability, Saturday and two evenings; can lift things; took a food safety unit in grade nine. He wrote nothing for "Tell me about yourself." His mother's injunction, delivered over the dishes, had been simple and impossible: be yourself. What he took from the video instead was a plan. Look the interviewer in the eye. Speak warmly. Let the face do the work.

On Tuesday Bryden came over with his bike helmet still buckled to his backpack and they set up in the kitchen, Bryden behind the counter as the interviewer, Aaron opposite. Bryden read questions off Aaron's phone in a flat voice, and Aaron answered with sustained eye contact and friendly, practiced nods. When Bryden asked what he'd do if a customer complained, Aaron smiled warmly and said something like "that would be handled appropriately," and Bryden's pen hovered over the paper and then wrote nothing. "I actually don't know what you just said," Bryden said. "You said it great, though. Very reassuring." Aaron laughed, but the laugh dried up when Bryden asked him again and Aaron realized he genuinely didn't have an answer. The face had nowhere to stand.

Maelle arrived Wednesday with chips and less patience. She took one look at Aaron's written plan, which now consisted of the words "eye contact" repeated three times, and asked where his actual answers were. When he recited the statistic, seven, thirty-eight, fifty-five, she frowned in a way that made him feel eleven years old. She had spent a weekend once going down the same rabbit hole for a class presentation on body language, and she remembered something that ruined his plan. The numbers came from a researcher named Albert Mehrabian, she said, and his experiments were about conveying feelings, whether a listener believed the emotion a speaker was showing. And she remembered, almost word for word, the part that mattered: Mehrabian himself said it does not apply to all communication. "So if I ask you how to stock a shelf," Maelle said, "your face can't stock it."

They tested it. Maelle asked Aaron, warmly and with admirable sincerity, what hours he could work, and Aaron responded only with an open, honest, deeply pleasant expression. She waited. She raised her eyebrows. She ate another chip. "Nothing," she reported. "I have learned nothing." But then she softened and pointed out what he'd gotten right without noticing: his eye contact had improved across three practice rounds, and his voice had stopped doing the thing where it climbed at the end of every sentence as though asking permission. He wasn't performing confidence badly; he just hadn't put anything inside the confidence yet.

So they spent Thursday morning writing actual answers, short ones, in words a person might really say, and Aaron rehearsed until the sentences stopped sounding borrowed. He read the grocery list off the fridge, imagined the dairy aisle, and wrote "I shop here with my mom, so I already know where things are," which Maelle declared the first thing on the page that sounded like him. His mother called from the hall to say the bus was in ten minutes. He stood in the kitchen doorway in his one collared shirt, and there was a moment where the two ideas stopped arguing and sat down together. The words carried the information; the eyes and the voice carried the person saying them. That seemed right. He still didn't know what he'd do if a customer complained, and that stayed with him like a stone in his shoe.

The office behind the customer service desk was small and smelled of cardboard and orange cleaner. The manager, a woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, asked why he wanted the job. Aaron looked at her, heard his own voice come out level, and said he shopped here with his mom and already knew where things were, and that he wanted the Saturday hours because school kept him busy the rest of the week. She wrote something down. Then she asked the question, the one he hadn't solved, about an angry customer, and Aaron felt the warmth drain out of his face and had to choose, fast, between a smooth nothing and a clumsy something.

"I don't know yet," he said. "I'd probably go get you." She looked up from her clipboard and gave him a noncommittal "hm," which could have meant anything, and Aaron held the eye contact anyway, hands folded on his knees, waiting to find out.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Tennessee Williams based Laura, the fragile sister in The Glass Menagerie, on his own sister Rose.
story:
Megan had written the same scene four times, and each time she had deleted it before the bell could catch her with it on the screen. The scene was true. That was the problem. Her older sister had come home in March, thin and quiet, and had sat at the kitchen table folding napkins into smaller and smaller squares while their mother stood at the stove pretending nothing had happened at the hospital. Mr. Huang had said the ten-minute play had to be staged from their own lives, that invention was for later, that first you learned what your actual material sounded like. Megan's material sat there in the cafeteria, two tables away, eating nothing.

"That bad?" Sammy asked, leaning over to look at the laptop. Megan tilted the screen away.

"It's my sister. The whole thing. If I stage it, everyone knows who she is."

Sammy stirred her yogurt. "So make her a stranger. Give her different hair."

"Then it's not her." Megan said it more sharply than she meant to, and Sammy raised an eyebrow, and Megan had to admit, at least to herself, that she did not know which she wanted more: to protect her sister or to finally say the thing out loud.

In sixth period, Braedon was blocking his own play in the corner of the black box theatre, moving chairs around to stand in for his father and his father's second wife.
