He was being facetious about it, giving the chairs notes in a mock director's voice, and Megan laughed even though she was watching how easily he did it, how he put his family on the floor and walked around them like they were furniture he was allowed to rearrange.

"How do you do that?" she asked, when he stopped for water.

"Do what?"

"Put him out there. Everyone's going to know it's your dad."

Braedon shrugged and dragged a chair into a new position. "You should look up Tennessee Williams," he said. "Mr. Huang told me about it when I was freaking out last week. There's a play called The Glass Menagerie."

That night Megan read instead of doing chemistry. The Glass Menagerie was about a family, a mother and her son and a daughter who was fragile, who kept tiny glass animals, who could not face the world. And Williams had based Laura, the fragile sister, on his own sister Rose. She read it twice on the screen, sitting very still on her bed while the house made its ordinary noises downstairs. He had done it. He had taken a real person, a real sister, and made her into a character named Laura, and the character was not a betrayal of the sister, or maybe she was, Megan could not tell from this distance. Rose had a life Megan knew nothing about. Laura had a life Megan was holding in her hands.

She sat with the laptop open to her half-deleted scene and thought about it for a long time. There was a version where staging her sister was a kind of theft, taking the worst month of someone else's life and turning it into a grade. There was a version where it was closer to what people did at funerals, eulogizing someone by saying exactly who they were, in public, with witnesses. And there was a third version she could not yet name, where the two were not opposites at all, where Williams putting Rose onstage was both a violation and an act of love, and no one, not even Rose, could have said where one ended and the other began. Megan did not have a considered position yet. What she had was a chair in a theatre and an unfinished page.

The next morning she found Braedon before first period and asked him how far was too far, how much of his father was in the play, and he said, "Enough that he'll recognize himself. Not enough that he can prove it." She said she did not want deniability. She wanted to be honest about who it was and honest that she did not know if she had the right.

In the black box that afternoon, Mr. Huang pulled two chairs to the centre of the floor and asked Megan what her play was about. She told him. The sister home from the hospital, the napkins, the mother at the stove. He asked who would play the sister, and Megan looked at the empty chair for a moment.

"I will," she said. "Sammy's going to read the mom. Braedon said he'd build the table."

Mr. Huang wrote something on his clipboard and asked where it started. Megan opened her notebook to the page she had rewritten at one in the morning, the one she had not deleted, and read the first line out loud: "She comes in with the napkins already in her hand, like she's been carrying them since March."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
story:
The living room had been cleared of everything except the couch, pushed against the window, and three folding chairs arranged where an imaginary audience would sit. Tyson stood where the audience sat and looked at the empty carpet, which was supposed to be a kitchen in suburban Ohio, and tried to see it that way. He had been chosen to direct the one-act because he had written it, and everyone assumed the two jobs could be subsumed under the same title, but by the second rehearsal he understood they were different animals. Directing meant telling people where to stand, and he had never once, in all his drafts, imagined where anyone stood.

"Okay," he said. "Selena, you come in downstage left."

Selena, who played the sister, stopped mid-line. "Why is it down? The floor's flat."

"It's not the floor," Tyson said. "Upstage means away from the audience, downstage means toward it."

"That makes no sense on a flat stage," she said, but she moved anyway, crossing the carpet toward the chairs, and something happened that Tyson had not expected. Her line landed differently when she was closer to him. It got louder without her raising her voice, and meaner, too, and he liked it.

Maximilien arrived late with a bag of chips and the scathing review of the previous night's rehearsal that he had apparently been composing all morning, mostly at Tyson's expense. "You said 'walk over there,'" he said, dropping into one of the audience chairs. "You pointed. You can't point in a real theatre. The actors will think you mean the lobby."

"I'm learning," Tyson said, and hated how it sounded, like an apology.

"You could just say upstage right," Maximilien said, crunching. "That's the back of the stage, right side. From our view, left."

From our view. Tyson had spent two days confused about that, until late last night, when Mr. Grant from next door had come over to borrow the ladder and found Tyson kneeling in the driveway with his notebook, drawing a rectangle. Mr. Grant had acted in community theatre for thirty years, and when Tyson asked him why the back of a flat stage was called up, Mr. Grant had laughed and said only that the old stages had been raked, sloped down toward the audience, and the names had stuck after the slopes were gone. Tyson had written it in the margin and then sat with it for a while. He liked that the words were fossils. Every rehearsal he ran, in a carpeted living room, was built on a stage that no longer existed, and everyone still obeyed its tilt.

But liking an idea was not the same as knowing what to do with it, and that was the part he couldn't explain to Maximilien, who wanted everything reduced to rules. Selena wanted the opposite. After Maximilien's critique, she pulled Tyson into the kitchen and said she thought the blocking was wrong for a deeper reason. "The sister wouldn't move toward him," she said. "She'd stay upstage. She's withdrawing. That's the whole scene."

"She has to cross," Tyson said. "The climax needs her in his face."

"That's your climax. Not hers."

He stood at the counter with his notebook and understood, slowly, that both of them were right and he would have to choose, or find a third thing. Maximilien's precision was a kind of respect for the audience, Selena's resistance was a kind of respect for the character, and a director, he decided, was the person who had to hold both at once without letting either one win by default. Whether he could actually do that, tonight, was a separate question. His father passed through for a glass of water, watched them arguing in whispers, and said nothing, which was its own form of mercy.

They ran the scene four more times. On the third, Tyson tried Selena's way, the sister retreating upstage, and felt the air go out of the room; the confrontation died politely, at a distance. On the fourth, he asked her to start far away and cross only on the last line, the cruelest one, so that she arrived downstage, inches from Maximilien's character, exactly as she said it. It worked, and Selena knew it worked, and she looked at him across the carpet without smiling, which was how she looked when she was satisfied. It wasn't a compromise, exactly. He had not split the difference; he had made the distance itself the meaning, the whole walk a sentence that ended on the word she spoke.

Afterward Maximilien gathered the chairs and said the metaphysics of it could wait until opening night, and Tyson let that pass without argument, because in a sense Maximilien was right. There was no way to know if any of it would hold under an audience that wasn't folding chairs. Selena found her jacket, then paused at the rectangle of cleared carpet, the imaginary kitchen, and stood for a moment at its far edge, facing out.

"This part's upstage," she said. "Even though it's the floor of your dad's living room."

"That's right," Tyson said.

She smiled then, just barely, and walked slowly downstage toward him, stopping a foot away, the way the sister would.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
The library had one outlet by the window, and Cohen had claimed it at nine in the morning with his laptop charger taped to the leg of the chair so nobody could trip on it and cut his power. The admissions portal auto-refreshed every sixty seconds. He had set it that way himself, which he now understood was a mistake, because every refresh the page went white and then blue again, and each time something in his chest dropped as though the answer might appear and then vanish before he could read it.

Johanna arrived at eleven with two coffees and slid one across the table without sitting down. "You're going to corrode," she said. "It posts at five, they said five, it's been five o'clock every year." She tapped his screen. "Also, you have to submit your reply to Alderman by midnight tomorrow. That's the actual deadline. You got in there, that's decided, that's a real thing that exists." She said it the way you'd remind someone water is wet, and Cohen said nothing, because he had already decided not to explain that Alderman was the safety, and a safety accepted was just proof you were the kind of person who needed one.

Zayd dropped into the chair beside her and pulled the second coffee toward himself, which started a short scuffle that ended with Johanna holding the cup above her head. "My cousin works tours at Wrenmore," Zayd said, once they'd settled. "He says their yield this year is the thing they brag about. I didn't know what he meant so I asked, and he told me straight." Zayd leaned in. "Yield is the percentage of students a college admits who actually accept the offer and enroll. That's it. That's the whole word."

"So it's like a store counting how many people who walk in buy something," Johanna said.

"Sure, except the people are you." Zayd turned his cup slowly on the table. "So when Wrenmore admits you, they're not only asking if they want you. They're betting on whether you'll come."

Cohen looked at his own reflection in the darkening screen. Last spring, before any of this, he had walked the Wrenmore campus with his father on a gray Saturday, and a tour guide in a green polo had bragged about the yield at the pond stop, under the big trees, and a senior near the front had raised a hand and asked what that meant. The guide's answer had gone in one ear and out the other; the arboreal shade, the smell of cut grass, his father's hand on his shoulder mattered more at the time. He had liked the campus the way you like a place you assume you'll never belong to. Now the word came back with edges on it. He was, at this moment, a percentage point in someone's spreadsheet either way: admitted and enrolling, or admitted and walking. The thought did not exactly enervate him, but it sat in his arms like a weight carried too far, that specific tiredness that has nothing to do with sleep.

He opened his email, because refreshing the portal was unbearable and email felt间接 like a side door. There was one message, from Mr. Zhao, who had coached his robotics team and who still, three months after graduation, sent notes that were two lines long. Cohen, it read. I owe you an apology. I told your father in October that the polymer project was a distraction from your applications. I have since read the paper you left in my mailbox. Your decision to test the adhesive with the wrong monomer on purpose, to see what the chain would not do, was better science than most of my undergraduates manage. Whatever school gets you gets a researcher. I am sorry I called it tinkering. Mr. Zhao. Cohen read it twice, then a third time, and Johanna watched his face change without asking why, which was the kindest thing anyone had done for him all day.

At four fifty he closed the lid partway so the hinge hid the screen, and Zayd said, "That's the opposite of refreshing." "I know," Cohen said. "That's the point." They worked on nothing, Johanna sketching a margin of geometric birds, Zayd reading the same paragraph of a chemistry textbook four times, and the library's big clock moved its hand the way clocks do when watched, in jumps that pretended to be smooth.

At five forty the page refreshed blue and stayed blue. Under Congratulations, there was a paragraph, and then a button that said Reply by May 1, and Cohen understood the button was asking two questions at once, do you want us and will you actually come, and that the college could not tell them apart and neither, right now, could he. Alderman's button waited too, in another tab, already sure of him. He reached past both and opened the polymer folder on his desktop, the one with the failed adhesive data, the one Mr. Zhao had called better science, and began drafting an email asking whether Wrenmore let first-years into materials labs. "You're not answering?" Johanna said. "Not yet," Cohen said, still typing. "I'm finding out what I'd be saying yes to."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A linear search checks items one by one from the start, so in the worst case, when the target is last or missing, it must look at every item.
story:
Amy had promised Ms. Ivanova the program by five o'clock, and at four fifteen it was still eating the afternoon. The roster file held nine thousand names, and the terminal in the library's back corner ticked through them the way water drips from a loose tap. She pressed return again and watched the cursor sit there, insolent, while Ayesha leaned over her shoulder.

"It's fast when I look up Nguyen," Amy said. "Half a second. But then I tried my own name."

"And?"

"And it's still thinking."

Ayesha pulled the second chair around and dropped into it. Outside the tall windows, the October light was turning the colour of weak tea. Paisley had claimed the table by the magazines and was pretending to study while eavesdropping, a habit she had never bothered to habituate herself out of, even after Ms. Ivanova had moved her seat twice in class.

"It doesn't like you," Ayesha offered. "That's the simplest theory."

"Thanks." Amy tabbed between two windows: her code in one, the roster in the other. The program walked the list from the top, comparing each name to the target, and something about that felt suddenly, embarrassingly obvious. It found Nguyen in three hundred steps because Nguyen sat near the front of the file. Her own name, Kowalski, sat near the bottom. Every name she had tested happened to be near the top, and she had let that flatter her. When the target was last, or missing entirely, the program had to look at every single item before it could say anything at all. She had spent an hour debugging logic that was never wrong. It was just doing everything the slow way, every time, on purpose.

"I know what it is," she said slowly, not wanting to say it aloud and make it real.

"Tell me."

"It checks one by one from the start. So when the name is at the end, or not in there at all, it checks all nine thousand. Every lookup I timed was easy. The hard ones, I never timed."

Ayesha frowned at the screen as though it had personally misled her, which in a sense it had. "So fix it."

"Ms. Ivanova said something in class last week." Amy closed her eyes, trying to retrieve it. "Binary search. You cut the list in half, then in half again. But it only works if the data is sorted, and I never checked whether the roster is sorted."

Paisley abandoned all pretence and came over, dragging her bag, an encumbrance of textbooks she refused to use the lockers for. "It's sorted," she said. "I checked Monday, for my own project. Alphabetical, all the way down."

Amy's pulse did something quick and unsteady. If the file was sorted, the fix was twenty minutes of work, and she could walk the program up to Ms. Ivanova's office before the building closed. She opened the roster and started scrolling, watching the surnames roll past in their long obedient parade, A through B, B through C. Paisley hovered. Ayesha chewed the end of a pen. The cursor in the other window had finally, at last, printed Not found.

"You see?" Paisley said. "Told you."

At the letter H, the parade stumbled. Hartley, Higgins, Herrera, then Hastings, then back to Hoffman, as if a clerk had dropped a card and slotted it in wrong. Amy stopped scrolling. She scrolled back and checked, and checked again, and the evidence was equivocal, one stray name in nine thousand, easily missed by anyone sampling the file instead of reading it, which was exactly what Paisley had done Monday and exactly what Amy would have done too, if she hadn't been hunting for reasons to distrust her own code.

"It's not sorted," Amy said. "There's a Hastings down in the H's."

Paisley leaned in, read it twice, and sat down hard on the arm of the chair. "That's not fair."

"No," Amy agreed. "It's not."

She sat for a moment with her hands off the keyboard, because the choice in front of her was not really about code. She could sort the file and run the fast search, and it would work, and Ms. Ivanova would never know the data had been dirty. Or she could write both versions, the honest slow one and the fast one, and bring the broken roster as evidence, and admit out loud that her earlier timings had meant nothing because she had only ever tested the easy cases. Ayesha was watching her with the particular stillness of someone who had already worked out what she was deciding.

"Which one are you doing?" Ayesha asked.

Amy opened a new file, typed a heading, and called up the library's clock in the corner of the screen. Four thirty-one.

"Both," she said, and started sorting.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In Canada outside Quebec, a typical paycheque shows deductions for income tax, Canada Pension Plan contributions and Employment Insurance premiums; Quebec uses its own pension and parental insurance plans.
story:
Kayla counted her tables twice before untying her apron, because the Saturday shift had felt longer than the money would justify. At the host stand she took her pay stub from Mr. Dang's folder, folded it once, and slid it into her back pocket, where it burned all through the dinner rush like a letter she was afraid to open. She had been saving for a deposit on an apartment in September, and the arithmetic in her head kept not working out.

At ten o'clock the restaurant emptied enough that Mr. Dang let two of them sit in a booth with soup that had gone tepid. Eden slid in across from her, still smelling of fryer grease, and Rory was already there, home for the weekend from Montreal, where he'd transferred in February to work in his uncle's place. He had his own pay stub out on the table next to the salt, turned so the fluorescent light caught the print.

"Read it and weep," Rory said. "Or read it and explain it to me, because I don't get it."

Kayla flattened her stub beside his. The two slips looked almost like the same document, the same grey type, the same columns, and then they weren't. Hers read Income Tax, then CPP, then EI, each with its own line subtracted from her gross. His read Income Tax too, but below that the lines changed, and where hers said Canada Pension Plan his said something else entirely, a provincial plan, and where hers said Employment Insurance his named a parental insurance plan instead.

"You got a different job title or something?" Eden asked, leaning over Kayla's shoulder. "Like, did you opt out?"

"You can't just opt out of CPP," Kayla said slowly, running her finger down his column. "I don't think. We're in Ontario. You're in Quebec. That's the whole difference, isn't it? Quebec has its own pension plan. And its own parental insurance thing instead of the EI line." She said it half as a question, because she had only ever seen her own stub, but the words sat right, the way a key sits when it starts to turn.

"So the deductions are the same everywhere in Canada," Rory said, "except where they're not."

"Except Quebec," Kayla said. "Outside Quebec it's like mine. Income tax, CPP, EI. In Quebec, those two bottom lines swap for their own plans." She was still not certain of every word of it, and she let that uncertainty stay, unhidden, the way she'd learned to in chemistry class: this much is solid, this much is fog.

Rory laughed and stabbed at his soup. The querulous voice of a woman at the counter drifted over, complaining that her bill showed more than the menu price, and Mr. Dang was explaining sales tax, pointing to the line where the provincial and federal amounts were added on top, the way tax rides on a receipt like a second passenger nobody invited. Kayla watched him circle it with a pen. On her own table's receipts that line had always looked like an accusation, but now she thought about how it was the same principle as the stubs: nothing arrived at its final number alone. Everything came delimited, bounded by what got taken off the top.

She took out her phone and opened the calculator, which was when the evening tilted. She had assumed, without ever saying it aloud, that Rory was simply ahead of her, that Montreal paid better, that he would make his deposit first and she would be the one explaining to her mother why September had to become October. But when she put his net pay beside his gross and did the same to her own, the proportions came out close enough that the difference came down to hours, not provinces, and she had worked more.

"Wait," she said. "How many shifts are you getting?"

"Six a week. Why?"

Kayla did the division twice. Her stub, which she had folded away in dread all night, showed fewer hours than she had actually worked. She stood up so fast the soup trembled in the bowl.

Mr. Dang was at the till, ringing out the complaining customer, counting her change into her palm with perfect courtesy. He looked up when Kayla reached the counter, and before Kayla could speak he said, "Before you ask. Your T4 slipped my mind, and the tax return season's over, so those hours will have to go on next pay." He smiled at the customer's retreating back, then at Kayla, and tapped the till.

"You mean," Kayla said, "you already know."

"Since Thursday," he said, and handed her a fresh copy of her stub, already corrected, from the folder he was still holding. She had been guarding the wrong piece of paper all night.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: DNA copying is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand.
story:
The calf was three days old and had decided that Ashley's boot was its mother, which meant Ashley had to stand very still in the corner of the barn while she recited from the index card in her hand. "DNA is transcribed into mRNA," she said, "and mRNA is translated into protein." The calf butted her ankle. She said it again, slower, the way Mr. Oyelaran had told her to, until the words stopped feeling like something borrowed. Around her the barn smelled of straw and iodine, and beyond the half-open door the October fields went from green to the pale gold of soybeans waiting for the combine.

She had taken the placement exam at the community college in August and failed the biology section by four points. Four points was the difference between starting the vet tech program in January and waiting a full year, and a year was a long time when you had already told everyone, including Kathleen at the diner, that you were leaving. The retake was on Saturday. Between now and then she had forty Jerseys, a job that started at five in the morning, and one evening a week when Mr. Oyelaran, the retired science teacher from the next road over, sat with her at his kitchen table and made her explain things until she could not hide behind vocabulary anymore.

Maci found her in the barn at noon, come to drop off the paperwork for the 4-H sale. She leaned over the rail and watched the calf gum Ashley's laces. "You're talking to it," Maci said. "You're actually standing there talking to a cow."

"She's a calf, and she doesn't judge." Ashley held up the index card. "I have to be able to explain this out loud. Not just recognize it on a test. Explain it, like to a farmer, like to someone who thinks it doesn't matter."

Maci took the card and squinted at it. "Transcription. Translation. Sounds like a bank robbery."

"That's actually not bad." Ashley came out of the pen and wiped her hands on her jeans. "Transcription is copying the message. The DNA stays in the nucleus, like the original file you never touch, and a copy gets made and carried out. Then translation is reading the copy, three letters at a time, and building a protein out of it. Every protein in that calf, the casein in the milk, the keratin in her hooves, came from instructions that got copied out and read."

Maci looked at the card again, then at the calf. "So the DNA in her, is that the same stuff that was copied when she was growing? Is it all new or is some of it old?" She said it lightly, the way she said most things, but Ashley went still.

The question landed in her like a stone in still water, because she had answered it once before and answered it wrong. It had been the junior class trip to the science museum in March, the one with the double helix sculpture in the lobby, big enough to walk under, its plastic base pairs clacking in the air conditioning. Two boys from the other high school had stood beneath it arguing, loudly enough that a docent drifted over. One of them said a copied DNA molecule was entirely new, a fresh build, the old one just a template that got discarded. The other said no, the copy kept the whole original somehow, like pressing flowers, the old molecule preserved whole inside the new. Ashley, peevish that day from the bus ride and from Kathleen sitting with someone else, had stepped in. She'd had biology the year before. She'd said it was all new, definitely, that was what copying meant, and she'd said it with the flat certainty of someone who wanted the argument to end more than she wanted to be right. The docent had started to speak and then a fire alarm had gone off, some kid pulling the handle on the third floor, and everyone had poured out onto the sidewalk and the moment dissolved. She had never found out. She had carried the not-knowing quietly for seven months, the way you carry a small debt you're embarrassed to collect on.

"Maci," she said now, "I think I got that wrong once. In front of people."

Maci raised an eyebrow and settled onto a hay bale, clearly willing to wait.

Ashley walked to the whiteboard Mr. Oyelaran had hung by the milk room, the one she used for scheduling the vet visits, and pulled the marker off its string. She drew the ladder, two rails and rungs. "When DNA copies itself, the two strands come apart." She split the ladder down the middle with her finger. "Each old strand stays whole. And each one becomes half of a new molecule. So the copy isn't all new and it isn't all old. Each new double helix keeps one strand from the original and pairs it with one newly built strand." She drew the new strands in, one beside each old rail. "There's a word for it. Semiconservative. Half conserved." She said the word twice, testing it, and something in her chest loosened. She had internalized it without meaning to, the way she had internalized the milking schedule and the sound the bulk tank made when the compressor was about to fail, by living inside the question instead of circling it.

"Like the farm," Maci said, surprising her. Maci's family had sold their acreage to a developer in the spring, and the corn had come out and the surveyor stakes had gone in, and her father had taken a job driving truck. She nodded at the whiteboard. "The old half stays. The new half gets built onto it. Nothing's all one thing anymore."

Ashley didn't say anything to that, because there was nothing to say that wouldn't sound like a sympathy card. She recapped the marker instead.

Mr. Oyelaran came through the barn at four for the evening ration and found the whiteboard covered in ladders and arrows, mRNA sketched floating off toward the milk room door with its little amino acids trailing behind it like ducklings. He read it in silence, hands in the pockets of his barn coat. He was not a man who praised, exactly; he was a man who withheld criticism, which those who knew him understood to be the same thing. "You could teach this," he said finally, and tapped the split helix. "You understand it better than you did in March."

"In March I was a reactionary," Ashley said. "Somebody said something loud and I just took the opposite side to make it stop." The calf had found its feet and was nosing along the rail toward the feed room. "I don't want to be that anymore."

He looked at her for a moment. "Saturday," he said. "Eight in the morning. Bring this whiteboard if you have to."

That night, after the last milking, Ashley sat on the overturned bucket by the calf pen and went through the stack of index cards one more time, but she kept stopping on the one with the split ladder drawn in her own handwriting. Passing on Saturday meant January meant leaving, and leaving meant Maci's family already gone and Kathleen at the diner sliding plates to strangers who would take Ashley's stool at the counter like it had never been hers. Staying meant the barn and the five a.m. light on the frost and the small hot breath of the calf against her palm. She did not know yet how the two halves of that paired up, which strand was the old one and which was being built new.

The calf shoved its nose into her pocket, hunting for a bottle that wasn't there.

"Not yet," Ashley told her.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: The ancient Greek historian Thucydides admitted that the speeches in his history of the Peloponnesian War were not word-for-word records, but what he judged each speaker would have needed to say.
story:
The monument stood at the edge of the park where the town buried its opinions: a granite soldier facing the school, a plaque listing the local dead from two wars, and a bench where Ms. Müller sat grading papers on warm afternoons. Abigail had chosen it as the site for her history project, a recorded recitation of Pericles' Funeral Oration, because she wanted the backdrop to mean something. She had practised the speech for two weeks, and the plan was simple: film herself at the soldier's base on Saturday morning, submit it, and win the regional prize that would look good on her college applications. That was the want, and it had a shape she could hold.

On Friday, Kristian sat across from her in the library, chin on his fist, listening to her run the opening lines for the fourth time. "You always pause after 'we are lovers of beauty,'" he said. "You think that's the important part?"

"It's the famous part," Abigail said. "Everyone knows it."

"Everyone knows the version that got quoted in the anthology," Kristian said. He slid his phone across the table. "My cousin took a classics course last year. She says Thucydides made half of it up. Or not made up exactly, but, look, read it yourself. I don't want to ruin your weekend."

She did not read it. She closed the phone, gathered her notes, and told him she would see him at the monument at nine. But she slept badly, and at eight in the morning she was standing outside Ms. Müller's classroom door before it opened, asking whether it was true, because Ms. Müller was the one adult in the school who would answer a question about dead Athenians before coffee.

Ms. Müller didn't give a speech. She pulled a battered paperback from her shelf, found the passage with a paper clip already marking it, and pushed it across the desk. "Read paragraph two. Then decide what you're doing today." Abigail read it standing up. Thucydides admitted that the speeches in his history of the Peloponnesian War were not word-for-word records, but what he judged each speaker would have needed to say. Not what Pericles said. What he would have needed to say. The words she had memorised were a historian's reconstruction, spoken in a voice that was half Thucydides, half the dead man, and no one alive could sort the halves.

She walked to the monument with the book in her bag and the camera in her hand, and Kristian was already on the bench, waiting, blowing into his cupped palms. The morning was grey, and the granite soldier looked jaundiced in that light, its weathered face more yellow than stone should be. "So you read it," Kristian said. Not a question.

"I read it. I'm still filming."

"Then what's the point of the pause after 'lovers of beauty'?"

"Maybe the pause is mine," she said, and heard how defensive it came out, and hated that it was also true in a way she hadn't examined.

They argued on the bench for twenty minutes while the camera sat unused on the soldier's base. Kristian wanted her to open with a disclaimer, an announcement that the words were invented; Abigail said that was too easy, a way of dichotomizing the speech into true or false when it was neither. "It's like this plaque," she said, pointing at the list of names. "Forty-one men from this town. That part's a record. But the sentence underneath says they died so we could be free. Who wrote that? Somebody after, deciding what the dead would have needed to stand for. Same instinct as Thucydides, just with worse prose."

Kristian was quiet for a moment. "So you're saying the monument's a lie?"

"No. I'm saying I don't know what to call it, and the disclaimer wouldn't fix that. It would just make me feel honest while saying nothing."

The light kept improving in small increments. She set up the camera, asked him to check the frame, and then stood in front of the soldier and found she could not start. The words were still there, every one memorised, but each now carried a second voice under it, the compiler's voice, and she stood in the cold while the camera recorded her silence. "Say why you chose it," Kristian called from behind the tripod. "First. Just say why." She looked at the names on the plaque, at the wreath some veterans' group had left in November and never collected, dried to the colour of paper.

She spoke to the lens. "I chose this speech because I thought it was the truest thing anyone ever said about a democracy honouring its dead. I still think it might be. But the man who wrote it down admitted it wasn't what was said, only what had to be said, and I've been trying all morning to decide whether that makes it less true or more." She paused where the famous pause had been, and then she began, "We are lovers of beauty," and let the rest of the oration go on without her knowing, in the end, which of them was speaking.

She filmed the whole thing once, told Kristian she would decide tonight whether to cut the introduction, and carried the camera home with the recording intact. At her desk she watched it twice. Then she opened Ms. Müller's paperback at the paper clip, read the admission a third time, and left the submission email unanswered in its tab. Her cursor blinked in the empty field for a long time before she typed, to Kristian, because he would understand the question better than the judges would: "If I send both, the disclaimer and the speech, does that ruin it or is that the only honest version?" His reply came as three dots that appeared, stopped, and appeared again.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: For ideal parallel plates, the field also equals the charge per unit area on a plate divided by the permittivity of free space, about 8.85 × 10^-12 farads per metre.
story:
The problem was due at midnight, and it was already past nine, and Sadie was sitting on the lip of the half-pipe with her phone balanced on her knee because the park was the only place where Abigale and Noah would actually help her instead of disappearing into their own homework. "Read it again," Abigale said, dropping onto the concrete beside her with her board clattering after. Sadie read it again. Two parallel plates, area given, charge given, find the field strength at a point between them. "It's a trick," Noah called from the bottom of the bowl, where he was attempting, and failing, something he called a fakie shove-it. "There's no voltage in it. You can't do it without the voltage."

"You can too," Sadie said, although at that moment she had no idea whether that was true. Her notebook page had the voltage formula crossed out twice, then crossed out a third time for emphasis, which was the kind of thing she did instead of solving problems. The online submission box would lock at midnight, and Ms. Lin had a policy about late work that Abigale described as "a disincentive so severe it counts as a threat."

Noah climbed up and sat on her other side, smelling like chalk dust and the energy drink he was too young to buy legally but somehow always had. He leaned over her notebook, then tapped the margin where she'd written her class notes in a shorthand only she could decode. "What's that bit say? The thing after 'for ideal plates.'" Sadie squinted at it. Her notes said, in her handwriting from Tuesday, when she'd been half-listening and half drawing a duck, that for ideal parallel plates the field also equals the charge per unit area on a plate divided by the permittivity of free space. Below it she'd copied the number: about 8.85 times 10 to the minus 12 farads per metre.

"Permittivity," Abigale said, tasting the word. "That sounds like something you'd get fined for." Sadie worked it fast. Charge per unit area: she divided the charge on the plate by the area, which the problem had thoughtfully given her, and then divided that by 8.85 times 10 to the minus 12. The number that came out was enormous, absurd, a field strength with a scientific notation that looked like a typo. "That can't be right," she said, and Noah said, "Put more zeros in," and Abigale said, "Put fewer," and neither of these was actual advice.

Here was where the two halves of Sadie's brain met, the half that trusted formulas and the half that trusted her own sense of when a number was ridiculous. She had spent four years treating those halves like roommates who refused to speak, and now, at a skate park at 9:40 p.m., she made them sit down at the same table. The formula said the answer was huge. Her gut said the answer was huge. Tiny charges on tiny plates, divided by a permittivity that was itself almost unimaginably small, and small divided by small could absolutely balloon outward. She checked the arithmetic a fourth time, mostly to externalize her nervousness onto the page instead of into her voice, because Abigale could smell doubt.

"It's right," she said. "I think it's actually right." Noah frowned at her notebook. "But you don't have the voltage. You never had the voltage." "You don't need it," Sadie said. "You can go around. There's a second door into the whole thing." She said it with more certainty than she had, which was a skill she'd learned from watching Ms. Lin answer questions in class: never let them see the decimal point wobble.

Then came the twist, which arrived at 10:15 in the form of a message from Ms. Lin in the class thread: the problem set would be open until Monday, since the site had been down all evening for half the students. Noah groaned loudly enough that a kid on a scooter turned to look. "We rushed for nothing," he said. "We panicked at a skate park for nothing." "Not nothing," Abigale said, and stole the last of his energy drink as ancillary compensation for her suffering.

Sadie didn't close her laptop, though. She sat with the answer on the screen, the big ridiculous number, and admitted to herself the part she hadn't said out loud: she was maybe ninety percent sure. There could be something about the point between the plates, some wrinkle in what "ideal" meant, that she was missing, and nobody here could tell her, and midnight could no longer tell her either. She thought about waiting until Monday and asking Ms. Lin point blank. She thought about the difference between a right answer you submitted and a right answer you understood.

She typed a note at the bottom of the box before she submitted: I used the charge per unit area divided by the permittivity of free space, about 8.85 times 10 to the minus 12 farads per metre, since there was no voltage given. Then she hit submit, at 10:31, with an hour and a half to spare that no longer mattered, and it felt better than waiting would have.

Noah picked up his board and pointed it at the bowl. "Physics lesson's over. Someone has to land a trick tonight, and it's statistically not going to be me." Sadie shut her laptop, stood, and stepped onto her board. "Show me the fakie thing again," she said. "Slowly."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A and E, from lowest to highest.
story:
Antoine had wanted the violin for exactly one reason, which was that his grandmother had played one, and after she died nobody in the family could tell him what her old case in the hall closet was worth beyond the smell of rosin and dust. Now he sat in Ms. Kowalski's studio every Tuesday at four, holding an instrument that felt like a small wooden animal resisting domestication. His neighbor on the folding chair beside him was Jana, who had started the same month he did, and who spent the first ten minutes of every lesson plucking strings and frowning at them as though they had lied to her.

"You're on the A again," Antoine said, when she reached for what she clearly thought was the D.

"I know what I'm doing." She plucked it anyway, heard the pitch climb instead of fall, and set the violin on her knee like a sulking child. "They all sound the same when I'm reading the music. The page says D and my hand just goes somewhere."

Ms. Kowalski, a dour woman in a cardigan the color of wet slate, moved between them and adjusted Jana's left elbow with two fingers, the way you'd nudge a picture frame level. She was not one for speeches. When she wanted something she said it in four words or fewer, and she believed, Antoine had gathered, that explanation was a kind of theft, that anything you could work out yourself belonged to you in a way nothing handed over ever would.

So she said only, "Fifths, from the bottom. Figure it out," and walked away to tune the piano in the corner, leaving the sentence behind her like a dropped glove.

Jana looked at Antoine. Antoine looked at his own strings, which he had been quietly memorizing for three weeks without admitting that he, too, lost his place. The lowest string, the fattest one, the one his grandmother's old recordings sat on, was G. He knew that much. He plucked it, then the one above it, and the second note rang out higher, and he remembered suddenly the tuning his uncle had let him listen to one night, the player sliding up and down the same interval again and again.

"G," he said slowly, plucking each string in turn, "then D, then A, then E. Going up. All the way to the highest one." He plucked the E, thin and bright as wire. "They're each a perfect fifth apart. That's what the tuning is. G, D, A, E, lowest to highest."

"So it's a pattern," Jana said. She was good at patterns, he knew; she was the one who had shown him how to memorize French verbs by grouping them into families. She laid her fingers lightly on the strings, one to each, like a pianist finding home keys. "G is the fat one at the bottom. Then you just climb. If I'm on the wrong string, the note will be a fifth off, and I'll hear it."

"It's like a lemma," Antoine said. He'd spent the weekend on calculus homework, and the word had stuck to him. "A little thing you prove first so the bigger thing works after."

"If you say so." But she was already plucking, muttering G, D, A, E under her breath like a spell, and when she misreached for a string her hand corrected itself before her eyes had even found the page.

Ms. Kowalski returned from the piano and stood behind them without saying anything, which was her version of applause. Then she set a duet on both their stands, a simple thing, one line each, and told them to sight read it together. Jana wanted to perform at the spring recital, she had told Antoine on the second Tuesday, her mother was coming up from the city for it, and this duet, he understood, was the audition. She played her first phrase cleanly, landed every note, and glanced at him with a quick, burning smile before the second phrase carried her on.

Antoine followed her, a little behind the beat, watching his own fingers and finding, with a small private astonishment, that they had learned something his mind hadn't yet noticed. Whether this would make him a violinist, whether he was doing it for his grandmother or for himself, whether those were even different things, he couldn't have said, and for the moment it didn't seem to matter. Ms. Kowalski turned the page for them both.

"Again," she said. "From the top, G to E."
